units.body:
Pillow: Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF ``` ============================================================================ Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDs Location: src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86 in MicImageFile.tell() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 5.6 KB image file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when an application asks how many frames the image has. This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package. Any application that opens an untrusted image and then reads `im.n_frames` can have one worker tied up indefinitely. That includes the common "is this image animated?" check and re-saving with `save_all=True` to TIFF, PDF or WebP. The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it. The file is a Microsoft Image Composer (MIC) container, which Pillow recognises by its magic bytes with no extension needed. Inside it is a TIFF stream with three chained image directories. `MicImageFile` subclasses `TiffImageFile` and overrides `seek()` and `tell()` so that a "frame" means one stream in the container. It still inherits `TiffImageFile.n_frames` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`), which walks the embedded TIFF's directory chain with `self._seek(self.tell() + 1)` until `_n_frames` is set. Two things stop that walk from making progress: - `MicImageFile.tell()` (`src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86`) returns the constant stream index. - `MicImageFile.seek()` calls `TiffImageFile._open()`, which resets `_n_frames` to `None`. As a result, the loop re-parses the second directory forever whenever the embedded stream has three or more directories. `Image.open()`, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in 0b33a87b0d15 (April 2020, first released in 7.2.0), which removed `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property. The attached reproducer builds the file in code and checks two controls, which return 3 and 1 frames as expected; the malicious file is still running when it is killed after 20 seconds. ## Details `MicImageFile` (registered for `Image.open` whenever `olefile` is installed) subclasses `TiffImageFile` and redefines a "frame" as one OLE `*.ACI/Image` stream, overriding `seek()` and `tell()` accordingly. It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs, and that implementation relies on `tell()` advancing as IFDs are loaded. `MicImageFile.tell()` returns the OLE stream index, which never changes inside `n_frames`, so the loop re-parses the same IFD forever. A 5632-byte OLE2 compound file whose `img0.ACI/Image` stream is a 351-byte TIFF with three chained 1×1 IFDs is enough. `Image.open()` on it succeeds (format `MIC`, detected by the OLE magic, no extension needed); evaluating `im.n_frames` then never returns and keeps one core at 100 %. A Python stack taken 27 s in is ``` File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1622 in _setup File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1271 in _seek File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1219 in n_frames ``` and instrumenting `_seek` shows it being called with `frame=1`, `tell()==0`, `_frame_pos==[8, 122]`, `_n_frames is None` on every iteration — identical state, so the loop is non-terminating, not merely slow. The same 351 TIFF bytes opened directly give `n_frames == 3` in milliseconds, and the same container around a 1-IFD TIFF gives `n_frames == 1`. The loop, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`: ```python @property def n_frames(self) -> int: current_n_frames = self._n_frames if current_n_frames is None: current = self.tell() self._seek(len(self._frame_pos)) while self._n_frames is None: self._seek(self.tell() + 1) # 1219 self.seek(current) ``` and the overrides that break its progress assumption, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:76`: ```python def seek(self, frame: int) -> None: … self.fp = self.ole.openstream(filename) TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) # 82: resets _n_frames to None self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: return self.frame # 87: OLE stream index, not TIFF __frame ``` For a plain TIFF, `_seek(k)` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1236`) loads IFDs up to `k`, appending each offset to `_frame_pos`, setting `_n_frames` when an IFD's next-pointer is 0 (or already seen), and setting the private `__frame = k`; `TiffImageFile.tell()` returns `__frame`, so `self.tell() + 1` walks the chain to its end. For a MIC file, `Image.open` → `MicImageFile._open` sets `self._n_frames = len(self.images)` at line 69, but then calls `self.seek(0)` → `TiffImageFile._open` (line 82), which unconditionally sets `self._n_frames = None` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1203`) and `_seek(0)`s into the embedded stream. With the 3-IFD stream, IFD 0 has a non-zero next pointer, so `_n_frames` stays `None` after open. `n_frames` then runs: `current = self.tell()` is `0` (the OLE index); `_seek(len(_frame_pos))` = `_seek(1)` loads IFD 1, whose next pointer is also non-zero and not yet in `_frame_pos`, so `_n_frames` is still `None`. The `while` body computes `self.tell() + 1` = `0 + 1` and calls `_seek(1)` again; `len(_frame_pos)` is already 2, so nothing new is loaded — IFD 1 is re-read via `tag_v2.load` and `_setup()` and the state is unchanged. This repeats indefinitely; IFD 2 is never reached. Two chained IFDs are not enough (IFD 1's next pointer of 0 sets `_n_frames = 2` on the first `_seek(1)`); three or more are. `Tests/test_file_mic.py::test_n_frames` passes only because `hopper.mic`'s stream has a single IFD, so `_seek(0)` sets `_n_frames = 1` and the loop is never entered; the `len(self.images)` assignment at line 69 is only consumed by the initial `_seek_check(0)` and is overwritten before any caller can read `n_frames`. A side effect of the same mismatch: with a 2-IFD stream `n_frames` returns 2 (TIFF IFDs) while `seek(1)` indexes `self.images[1]` (OLE streams) and raises `IndexError` — visible with `save_all=True`. ## Impact Any application that lets Pillow open an uploaded file and then reads `im.n_frames` — the usual way to decide whether an image is animated (`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) > 1`), and also what `hasattr(im, "n_frames")`/`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1)` in Pillow's own `TiffImagePlugin._save_all` (`:2333`), `PdfImagePlugin._save` (`:250`) and `WebPImagePlugin._save_all` (`:171`) evaluate when the app re-saves with `save_all=True` — can be made to spin one worker at 100 % CPU indefinitely with a 5.6 KB upload. The file needs no particular extension (OLE magic; `FpxImagePlugin` rejects it on CLSID and `MicImagePlugin` accepts it), default limits do not intervene, memory does not grow, and no exception is raised, so only an external watchdog ends it. Preconditions: `olefile` installed (it is an optional dependency; without it the MIC plugin is not registered) and the application touching `n_frames` or a `save_all` path. `Image.open()` itself, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. This is the same class of tiny-file, pure-Python non-termination as CVE-2021-28676 (FLI) and CVE-2021-28677 (EPS), and like CVE-2019-19911 (FPX) it depends on `olefile`; it differs in not being reached by the default open/load path. The regression was introduced in `0b33a87b0d15` ("Replaced property methods for n_frames and is_animated with normal properties", 2020-04-13), first released in 7.2.0, which replaced `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property with the `_n_frames` attribute that `TiffImageFile._open` overwrites. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (with `olefile`, which is what registers the MIC plugin). It builds every input in code, writes each one to a temporary file named `x` with no extension (so Pillow identifies the format from its magic bytes), and opens it in a child Python process that runs `Image.open(path)` and prints `im.format` and `im.n_frames`. It builds two things in code: - `tiff(n)`: an `n`-page TIFF of 4×4 greyscale frames written by Pillow itself (`save_all=True`), so the IFDs are chained exactly as Pillow's own writer chains them. The last next-IFD pointer is 0. - `mic(stream)`: a minimal OLE2 compound file with a storage named `img0.ACI` that contains a stream named `Image`, which is the layout `MicImageFile._open` looks for. Sector 0 is the FAT and sector 1 is the directory. The stream starts at sector 2 and is padded to 4096 bytes, so the file doesn't need a mini-FAT. The result is 5632 bytes. It runs three inputs, each in its own child process with a hard 20-second kill: 1. control: the plain 3-page TIFF. Expected `TIFF n_frames = 3`. 2. control: a MIC wrapping a 1-page TIFF. Expected `MIC n_frames = 1`. 3. attack: the same MIC container wrapping the 3-page TIFF. The timeout is enforced by killing the child rather than by an in-process alarm, because a `TimeoutError` raised while `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` is parsing would be caught by its `except OSError` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:958`) and leave the IFD half-parsed instead of stopping the loop. The script prints `BUG` when both controls return and the attack child is still running after 20 seconds; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, the attack case prints `MIC n_frames = 1` and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch restores the OLE-level frame count after the embedded TIFF stream has been opened, so the inherited `n_frames` never enters its IFD-walking loop and `n_frames`/`seek()` agree on what a frame is. In `MicImageFile.seek`, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:82`, right after `TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self)`: ```diff TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame ``` Doing this in `seek()` restores the invariant on every seek, not only the first. The existing assignments at lines 69–70 of `_open` are kept: the initial `seek(0)` → `_seek_check(0)` reads `n_frames` before `TiffImageFile._open` has run, so they are still needed. Plain read-only `n_frames`/`is_animated` properties, as before 0b33a87b0, are no longer a drop-in option because `TiffImageFile._seek` assigns `self.is_animated`. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the attack file returns `n_frames == 1` immediately, a 2-IFD stream raises `EOFError` on `seek(1)` instead of `IndexError`, `save_all=True` to TIFF and PDF completes, and `Tests/test_file_mic.py` and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py` pass. No regression test is included, since one would need a new binary MIC fixture in `Tests/images`. The patch passed that check but has not been reviewed beyond it as the final form of the fix. Two things it leaves alone: it does not add the `_im` reset that `TiffImageFile.seek` performs after `_seek` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1229`), which matters when switching between OLE streams of different size or mode; and `TiffImageFile.n_frames` still advances via the overridable `tell()` rather than its private `__frame`, so making it iterate on `__frame` would protect any other subclass that redefines `tell()`. ## The patch Restore the OLE stream frame count in MicImageFile.seek() after TiffImageFile._open() resets it, so n_frames cannot loop forever Applies to `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. It passed the mechanical check — applied to a clean tree, rebuilt, the reproducer stopped firing — but a reviewer did not endorse it as the right fix. ```diff diff --git a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py index f8cf3a76f..2bb0109ce 100644 --- a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py @@ -81,6 +81,11 @@ class MicImageFile(TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile): TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,330 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # MicImageFile inherits TiffImageFile.n_frames, whose loop `self._seek(self.tell()+1)` # relies on tell() advancing; MicImageFile.tell() returns the OLE stream index (constant), # so a MIC file whose Image stream is a TIFF with >=3 chained IFDs makes im.n_frames spin forever. import io, struct, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os from PIL import Image def tiff(n): # n-page TIFF written by Pillow itself b = io.BytesIO(); fr = [Image.new("L", (4, 4), i) for i in range(n)] fr[0].save(b, "TIFF", save_all=True, append_images=fr[1:]); return b.getvalue() def mic(stream): # minimal OLE2 file: storage "img0.ACI" containing stream "Image" END, FREE, FATSECT = 0xFFFFFFFE, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFD data = stream.ljust(4096, b"\0"); n = len(data) // 512 fat = [FATSECT, END] + [3 + k for k in range(n - 1)] + [END]; fat += [FREE] * (128 - len(fat)) def entry(name, kind, child, start, size): raw = name.encode("utf-16-le") + b"\0\0" return raw.ljust(64, b"\0") + struct.pack(" {out}"); return hung c1 = run("control: 3-page TIFF, direct", tiff(3)) c2 = run("control: MIC around 1-page TIFF", mic(tiff(1))) bug = run("attack: MIC around 3-page TIFF", mic(tiff(3))) print("BUG" if bug and not c1 and not c2 else "OK") ```
---

Pillow: BMP RLE decoder memory-amplification DoS via unbounded delta escape / absolute mode
## Summary
BmpRleDecoder can be forced to allocate gigabytes of memory from a kilobyte-sized crafted BMP file via unbounded growth in the delta escape and absolute mode branches.

## Affected versions
All versions up to and including current HEAD (v13.0.0.dev0, commit e7a7ea84)

## Root cause
BmpRleDecoder.decode() (BmpImagePlugin.py:327-395) builds a Python bytearray `data` with dest_length = xsize*ysize, looping `while len(data) < dest_length`. The loop condition is only checked at the TOP; individual branches append attacker-controlled amounts UNBOUNDED by dest_length:

- delta escape (line 370): data += b"\x00" * (right + up * self.state.xsize) with right,up in 0..255 -> up to ~255*xsize bytes in ONE iteration.
- absolute mode (line 385): data += bytes_read (up to 255).

Because a single delta can push len(data) to ~256 * (row size), a tiny RLE stream combined with a large-but-legal xsize (xsize*ysize just under MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, ~89M) yields a multi-GB `data` bytearray (then copied again by bytes(data) and set_as_raw). No heap OOB (bytearray/set_as_raw are bounds-safe), but a severe memory-amplification DoS: the attacker file stays tiny.

## Reproduction
Python 3.13, Pillow HEAD e7a7ea84

Attached: pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py

A 1084-byte BMP (BI_RLE8, width=3,000,000, height=1 -> 3M px, passes bomb check) with one delta escape (00 02 00 150) produces ~429 MB `data`; measured peak RSS 911 MB. Scaling width toward the bomb limit and up=255 produces tens of GB from a ~1 KB file.

## Suggested fix
Cap growth at dest_length in the delta and absolute branches, e.g. clamp the delta fill to (dest_length - len(data)) and stop appending once len(data) >= dest_length; reject deltas that would move the cursor beyond the image, matching the existing per-row clamp at line 341-343.

Credit: Yazan Balawneh - CyStack Security Team (GitHub: sonicnew)

[pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30244974/pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py)

Pillow: PdfParser can recurse without limit in get_value() and linearize_page_tree()
### Summary
`PdfParser`'s `get_value()` can recurse without any limit and crash with an uncaught `RecursionError`. It is reachable through `Image.save(im, fp=<pdf>, format="PDF", append=True)` when the existing PDF file is attacker-controlled. This is the same class of bug as https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 (the /Prev trailer chain loop, fixed earlier this year), in the same file, but in two different functions that fix did not touch.

### Details
**`get_value()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`**

This is a classmethod that takes `max_nesting: int = -1` and has a guard:

```python
if max_nesting == 0:
    return None, None
```

Every recursive call (nested arrays, dictionaries, indirect object definitions) passes `max_nesting=max_nesting - 1`. Since the default and every call site start at -1, this only ever counts down further negative: -1, -2, -3, and so on. It never equals exactly 0, so the guard never runs. A PDF object with a value nested a few thousand levels deep is enough to hit Python's recursion limit. It does not even need a valid `/Pages` tree, since `read_pdf_info()` parses the `/Root` object's own dictionary first, before checking anything else.

This advisory reports a single vulnerability: an ineffective recursion-depth guard in `PdfParser.get_value()` (the sentinel  `-1`  default never reaches the `== 0` check). The mention of GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 is comparative context for an already-fixed, already-CVE'd bug in a different function — it is not a second vulnerability being reported. The three trigger paths (nested arrays/dicts/indirect objects) are not independently fixable; they share one root cause and one fix location in  get_value() .

### Steps to reproduce
Both PDFs below are plain text, built directly in Python, no PDF library needed.

```python
from PIL.PdfParser import PdfParser

def build_pdf(root):
    out = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4\n")
    offset = len(out)
    out += f"1 0 obj\n".encode()
    out += root
    out += b"\nendobj\n"
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    xref_offset = len(out)
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    out += b"trailer\n"
    out += f"<< /Size 2 /Root 1 0 R >>\n".encode()
    out += b"startxref\n"
    out += f"{xref_offset}\n".encode()
    out += b"%%EOF"
    return bytes(out)

bomb = b"[" * 3000 + b"]" * 3000
root = b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R /Bomb " + bomb + b" >>"
with open("nesting_bomb.pdf", "wb") as f:
    f.write(build_pdf(root))

PdfParser("nesting_bomb.pdf")     # raises RecursionError
```

Expected: a clean `PdfFormatError`.

Actual: raises a raw `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`.

### Impact
- Availability: an attacker who controls the content of a PDF file that an application later appends an image page to (`Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`) can crash that request with a RecursionError, using a file of a few hundred bytes.
- Confidentiality: none.
- Integrity: none.
- Pillow cannot open PDFs for reading through `Image.open()`. `PdfParser` is only reached through the append-mode save path, so the app has to be doing that specific thing (for example, stamping or watermarking an existing PDF) for this to matter.

units.body:
Cross-site Scripting in Apache Struts
When the Struts2 debug mode is turned on, under certain conditions an arbitrary script may be executed in the 'Problem Report' screen. Also if JSP files are exposed to be accessed directly it's possible to execute an arbitrary script. 

It is generally not advisable to have debug mode switched on outside of the development environment. Debug mode should always be turned off in production setup. Also never expose JSPs files directly and hide them inside WEB-INF folder or define dedicated security constraints to block access to raw JSP files.

Struts >= 2.3.20 is not vulnerable to this attack. We recommend upgrading to Struts 2.3.20 or higher if turning off debug mode is not possible.

units.body:
Pillow: NULL dereference in ImagingExpand via rank filters on zero-size images ``` ============================================================================ NULL dereference in ImagingExpand via rank filters on zero-size images Location: src/libImaging/Filter.c:79 in ImagingExpand() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Applying Pillow's median, minimum, maximum or rank filter to an image with zero width or zero height crashes the whole Python process instead of raising an error. Empty images like this are easy to produce with ordinary calls, for example a crop box whose left and right edges (or top and bottom edges) are equal, or the second page of a crafted multi-page image file. An attacker who can supply crop coordinates or an uploaded file to an application that runs one of these filters can kill its worker process. The effect is a crash only, with no memory disclosure or corruption. The fault is in `ImagingExpand()` in `src/libImaging/Filter.c`. This is the edge-padding step that `RankFilter.filter()` always runs through the core `expand()` method, so `MedianFilter`, `MinFilter` and `MaxFilter` go through it too. It fills the margin by copying the input's edge pixels, reading `imIn->image[y][0]` and rows `0` / `ysize-1`, and never checks that the input has any pixels. For an empty image, `ImagingAllocateArray` leaves the line pointers NULL, so the first read dereferences NULL and the process dies with SIGSEGV, in every mode. Zero-size images reach this point through public API alone: - `Image.crop()`, `ImageOps.crop()` and `Image.new()`; - a multi-page TIFF opened by path whose second IFD declares `ImageLength = 0`, on which `seek(1)` and `load()` succeed. Every other `ImageFilter` returns an empty image for the same inputs. The zero-height case has crashed since the original PIL import, and the zero-width case since Pillow 4.3.0. This is separate from the `margin == 0` fix in #9755: the path is the same, but here the degenerate value is the image size rather than the kernel size. It has the same shape as the zero-dimension `ImagingOffset` crash fixed under GHSA-f87v-9578-p47w. The attached reproducer shows a one-pixel-wide control crop filtering normally, while four empty crops passed through the rank filters are each killed by SIGSEGV. A patch that returns early in `ImagingExpand` for empty input is included. ## Details `ImagingExpand()` (`src/libImaging/Filter.c`), the edge-padding helper that `ImageFilter.RankFilter` runs before the actual rank filter, reads the first pixel of each input line without checking that the input has any pixels. For an image with width 0 or height 0 the line pointers are NULL, so `Image.filter()` with `MedianFilter`, `MinFilter`, `MaxFilter` or `RankFilter` kills the interpreter with SIGSEGV instead of returning or raising: ```python from PIL import Image, ImageFilter im = Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop((3, 0, 3, 10)) # size (0, 10); crop() accepts left == right im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3)) # SIGSEGV ``` Under gdb on the stock build the fault is at `ImagingExpand (imIn=…, margin=1) at src/libImaging/Filter.c:105` (the `EXPAND(UINT8, image8)` expansion), called from `_expand_image` at `src/_imaging.c:1151`, with `imIn->xsize = 0` and `imIn->image[0] = 0x0`. The same happens for every mode the rank filters accept (`L`, `RGB`, `RGBA`, `I`, `F`), and the core `expand(m)` method with `m >= 1` crashes the same way in any mode, including `P`. The same input through `BoxBlur`, `GaussianBlur`, `Kernel`, `ModeFilter` and `UnsharpMask` returns a `(0, 10)` image; a `(1, 10)` crop through `MedianFilter` also returns normally. The unchecked edge reads date from the PIL import (`9a640e315`, 2010, so every Pillow release): the zero-height case has crashed since then, and the zero-width case since `fd907fbdc` ("Fix 0-width and 0-height images other way", Pillow 4.3.0), which stopped backing zero-width images with a dummy block and left their row pointers NULL. It is adjacent to the `margin == 0` divide-by-zero fix in #9755 — same `expand()` → `ImagingExpand()` path, but the unhandled degenerate value here is the image size rather than the kernel size. The path: ```python # src/PIL/ImageFilter.py:111-116 RankFilter.filter (MedianFilter/MinFilter/MaxFilter subclass it) image = image.expand(self.size // 2) return image.rankfilter(self.size, self.rank) ``` `expand(m)` with `m > 0` is `ImagingExpand(self->image, m)` (`src/_imaging.c:1142-1151`). It validates only `margin`, allocates an output of `(xsize+2*margin) × (ysize+2*margin)` — which is non-empty, so the allocation succeeds — and then fills the margin by replicating edge pixels of the input: ```c // src/libImaging/Filter.c:70-101 imOut = ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); … #define EXPAND_LINE(type, image, yin, yout) \ { \ for (x = 0; x < margin; x++) { \ imOut->image[yout][x] = imIn->image[yin][0]; \ // line 79 } \ … \ for (x = 0; x < margin; x++) { \ imOut->image[yout][margin + imIn->xsize + x] = \ imIn->image[yin][imIn->xsize - 1]; \ // [-1] when xsize == 0 } \ } #define EXPAND(type, image) \ { \ for (y = 0; y < margin; y++) { \ EXPAND_LINE(type, image, 0, y); \ // line 0 of a 0-line image } \ … for (y = 0; y < margin; y++) { \ EXPAND_LINE(type, image, imIn->ysize - 1, margin + imIn->ysize + y); \ // line -1 when ysize == 0 } \ } ``` Why the line pointers are NULL: `ImagingNewPrologueSubtype` callocs the `im->image` pointer array (`src/libImaging/Storage.c:216`, at least one entry), and `ImagingAllocateArray` returns before assigning any of them for an empty image: ```c // src/libImaging/Storage.c:423-426 /* 0-width or 0-height image. No need to do anything */ if (!im->linesize || !im->ysize) { return im; } ``` So with `xsize == 0` every `imIn->image[y]` is NULL and `imIn->image[yin][0]` faults; with `ysize == 0` the top-margin pass reads `imIn->image[0]` (the single calloc'd NULL slot) and faults the same way, and the bottom-margin pass would index `imIn->image[-1]`. `ImagingRankFilter` is never reached. Zero-size images are ordinary objects in Pillow and arrive at `filter()` through public API only: - `Image.crop(box)` rejects only inverted boxes (`src/PIL/Image.py:1385-1390`); `left == right` or `upper == lower` yields a 0×N / N×0 image. `ImageOps.crop(im, border)` with `border == width // 2`, and `Image.new(mode, (0, n))`, do the same. - From a file: `ImageFile.__init__` refuses a zero first-frame size (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:167-173`), but `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` takes `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` of every later IFD as-is on `seek()` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1468-1481`). For an uncompressed page of an image opened by path, `ImageFile.load()` takes the mmap branch (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:307, 325-347`) and `Image.core.map_buffer` builds an `8×0` core image without complaint (`src/map.c:127-141`), so `im.seek(1); im.load()` succeeds and a following `im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3))` segfaults in `ImagingExpand` exactly as above (verified under gdb: `imIn->ysize = 0`, `imIn->image[0] = 0x0`). A 384-byte two-page TIFF is enough. ## Impact Denial of service: the whole embedding process (web worker, pipeline process) dies with SIGSEGV rather than the request failing with a Python exception. It is reachable by a remote user in two realistic shapes: (a) an application that crops an upload to user-supplied coordinates and then applies a median/min/max filter (denoise, dilate/erode, thumbnail clean-up) — a box with `x0 == x1` or `y0 == y1` passes `crop()` and crashes the worker; (b) an application that opens an uploaded TIFF from disk by path, iterates its pages and applies a rank filter to each — a crafted second IFD with `ImageLength = 0` crashes it. The faulting access is a read at address 0 (or a fixed small negative offset from the pointer array for the `[-1]` cases, which is not reached because the first read already faults), so there is no memory disclosure or corruption beyond the crash. The same shape, a zero-dimension image crashing C code reached through public API, was fixed in `ImagingOffset` in 39d14a0db (GHSA-f87v-9578-p47w). ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow as-is (no rebuild). It runs each case in a fresh child interpreter, with core dumps disabled. That way a segfault shows up as the child's exit status and the script itself keeps running. Each child builds `Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop(box)`, prints its size, calls `im.filter(...)` and then prints the size of the result. - **Control**: a `(1, 10)` crop (`(3, 0, 4, 10)`) through `MedianFilter(3)`. The rank filter accepts a thin image and must return normally. - **PoC**: the rank filters on empty crops. - A `(0, 10)` crop (`left == right`, `(3, 0, 3, 10)`) through `MedianFilter(3)` and `MaxFilter(5)`. - A `(10, 0)` crop (`upper == lower`, `(0, 3, 10, 3)`) through `MinFilter(3)`. - A `(0, 0)` crop (`(3, 3, 3, 3)`) through `RankFilter(3, 4)`. Expected output on the stock build: ``` crop(3, 0, 4, 10) MedianFilter(3) (1, 10) -> (1, 10) crop(3, 0, 3, 10) MedianFilter(3) (0, 10) -> killed by SIGSEGV crop(3, 0, 3, 10) MaxFilter(5) (0, 10) -> killed by SIGSEGV crop(0, 3, 10, 3) MinFilter(3) (10, 0) -> killed by SIGSEGV crop(3, 3, 3, 3) RankFilter(3, 4) (0, 0) -> killed by SIGSEGV BUG ``` The size printed before `->` shows that the empty image was created without error. The crash happens inside `filter()`, in `ImagingExpand`. The last line is `BUG` if the control returned normally and at least one rank-filter child was killed by SIGSEGV. Otherwise it is `OK`. The script covers the crop route only; the TIFF route described above fails the same way (`im.seek(1); im.load(); im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(3))` on a by-path two-page TIFF whose second IFD has `ImageLength = 0`). With the attached patch, every PoC line prints the unchanged size (for example `(0, 10) -> (0, 10)`) and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch handles the empty input in `ImagingExpand` (`src/libImaging/Filter.c`), right after the `margin` checks and before the `ImagingNewDirty` allocation and the replication loops. With `xsize == 0` or `ysize == 0` there are no edge pixels to replicate, so it returns a zeroed (`ImagingNew`, not `ImagingNewDirty`) image of the expanded size, with the input's palette copied. This keeps `ImagingExpand`'s size contract, so `ImagingRankFilter` then produces an output of `xsize - 2*margin` × `ysize - 2*margin`, i.e. the original empty size, matching every other filter. It mirrors the existing zero-dimension early returns in `src/libImaging/BoxBlur.c` (127004368) and `src/libImaging/Offset.c` (39d14a0db): ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/Filter.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Filter.c @@ -67,6 +67,17 @@ ImagingExpand(Imaging imIn, int margin) { return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("filter size too large"); } + if (imIn->xsize == 0 || imIn->ysize == 0) { + /* No edge pixels to replicate (and no lines to read from), so + return a zeroed image of the expanded size */ + imOut = ImagingNew(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); + if (!imOut) { + return NULL; + } + ImagingCopyPalette(imOut, imIn); + return imOut; + } + imOut = ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); if (!imOut) { ``` The patch also adds `test_rankfilter_zero_dimension` next to `test_rankfilter_error` in `Tests/test_image_filter.py`, which filters `Image.new("L", size)` for `size` in `((0, 6), (6, 0), (0, 0))` with `MinFilter`, `MedianFilter`, `MaxFilter` and `RankFilter(3, 2)` and asserts the size is preserved. Applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer prints `OK` and `Tests/test_image_filter.py` passes. A Python-level guard in `RankFilter.filter` (`if 0 in image.size: return image.copy()`) would also stop the crash, but the C-level check protects any other caller of `expand()`. ## The patch Return a zeroed image from ImagingExpand when the input has zero width or height instead of reading NULL line pointers Applies to `src/libImaging/Filter.c` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_image_filter.py b/Tests/test_image_filter.py index 974d4b7a3..8dc8e1a1a 100644 --- a/Tests/test_image_filter.py +++ b/Tests/test_image_filter.py @@ -155,6 +155,23 @@ def test_rankfilter_error(filter: ImageFilter.RankFilter) -> None: im.filter(filter).getpixel((1, 1)) [email removed]( + "filter", + ( + ImageFilter.MinFilter, + ImageFilter.MedianFilter, + ImageFilter.MaxFilter, + ImageFilter.RankFilter(3, 2), + ), +) [email removed]("size", ((0, 6), (6, 0), (0, 0))) +def test_rankfilter_zero_dimension( + filter: ImageFilter.RankFilter, size: tuple[int, int] +) -> None: + im = Image.new("L", size) + assert im.filter(filter).size == size + + def test_rankfilter_properties() -> None: rankfilter = ImageFilter.RankFilter(3, 2) diff --git a/src/libImaging/Filter.c b/src/libImaging/Filter.c index 3492a871f..d702db5f9 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Filter.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Filter.c @@ -67,6 +67,17 @@ ImagingExpand(Imaging imIn, int margin) { return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("filter size too large"); } + if (imIn->xsize == 0 || imIn->ysize == 0) { + /* No edge pixels to replicate (and no lines to read from), so + return a zeroed image of the expanded size */ + imOut = ImagingNew(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); + if (!imOut) { + return NULL; + } + ImagingCopyPalette(imOut, imIn); + return imOut; + } + imOut = ImagingNewDirty(imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * margin, imIn->ysize + 2 * margin); if (!imOut) { ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,333 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Pillow: rank filters (Median/Min/Max/RankFilter) on a 0-wide or 0-high image # SIGSEGV in ImagingExpand (src/libImaging/Filter.c) - NULL line pointer read. # Each case runs in a child interpreter; BUG if the control returns and any # zero-size case dies of SIGSEGV. import signal, subprocess, sys CHILD = """ import resource; resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CORE, (0, 0)) from PIL import Image, ImageFilter im = Image.new("L", (10, 10)).crop(%s) # public API; crop accepts x0==x1 / y0==y1 print(im.size, "->", end=" ", flush=True) print(im.filter(ImageFilter.%s).size) """ def run(box, flt): p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", CHILD % (box, flt)], capture_output=True, text=True) out = p.stdout.strip() if p.returncode < 0: out += " killed by " + signal.Signals(-p.returncode).name print(f" crop{box!s:<16} {flt:<18} {out}") return p.returncode ctrl = run((3, 0, 4, 10), "MedianFilter(3)") # (1,10): must work rcs = [run((3, 0, 3, 10), "MedianFilter(3)"), # (0,10) run((3, 0, 3, 10), "MaxFilter(5)"), run((0, 3, 10, 3), "MinFilter(3)"), # (10,0) run((3, 3, 3, 3), "RankFilter(3, 4)")] # (0,0) bug = ctrl == 0 and any(rc == -signal.SIGSEGV for rc in rcs) print("BUG" if bug else "OK") ```

units.body:
urllib3 streaming API improperly handles highly compressed data
### Impact

urllib3's [streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/2.5.0/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o) is designed for the efficient handling of large HTTP responses by reading the content in chunks, rather than loading the entire response body into memory at once.

When streaming a compressed response, urllib3 can perform decoding or decompression based on the HTTP `Content-Encoding` header (e.g., `gzip`, `deflate`, `br`, or `zstd`). The library must read compressed data from the network and decompress it until the requested chunk size is met. Any resulting decompressed data that exceeds the requested amount is held in an internal buffer for the next read operation.

The decompression logic could cause urllib3 to fully decode a small amount of highly compressed data in a single operation. This can result in excessive resource consumption (high CPU usage and massive memory allocation for the decompressed data; CWE-409) on the client side, even if the application only requested a small chunk of data.


### Affected usages

Applications and libraries using urllib3 version 2.5.0 and earlier to stream large compressed responses or content from untrusted sources.

`stream()`, `read(amt=256)`, `read1(amt=256)`, `read_chunked(amt=256)`, `readinto(b)` are examples of `urllib3.HTTPResponse` method calls using the affected logic unless decoding is disabled explicitly.


### Remediation

Upgrade to at least urllib3 v2.6.0 in which the library avoids decompressing data that exceeds the requested amount.

If your environment contains a package facilitating the Brotli encoding, upgrade to at least Brotli 1.2.0 or brotlicffi 1.2.0.0 too. These versions are enforced by the `urllib3[brotli]` extra in the patched versions of urllib3.


### Credits

The issue was reported by @Cycloctane.
Supplemental information was provided by @stamparm during a security audit performed by [7ASecurity](https://7asecurity.com/) and facilitated by [OSTIF](https://ostif.org/).

units.body:
Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO
```
============================================================================
Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO
Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:94  in _tiffWriteProc()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

Pillow can write attacker-chosen data past the end of a heap buffer when it saves a TIFF image to an in-memory destination such as `io.BytesIO` rather than to a file. The same code also copies leftover heap memory from the process into the saved file. Anyone who can supply an image to a service that opens it and re-saves it as TIFF this way can trigger this with default settings. The attached reproducer crashes the process, and the overflow could potentially be developed further, but code execution is not demonstrated here.

The bug is in `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. This is the write callback for the in-memory sink that Pillow gives libtiff whenever the save target has no `fileno()`. While writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the current end of data and writes tag values there. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of from the write position `state->loc`. As a result, the first out-of-line tag value written after that seek can run past the allocation by up to the size of the directory: 12 bytes per entry, 126 bytes in the minimal case, and 2384 bytes observed with a 331-entry directory. The overflowing bytes are the tail of a tag value taken from the uploaded file.

No save options are needed, because compression and tags are inherited from the source image. The overflow does require an attacker-sized out-of-line tag to reach libtiff. That happens when the opened TIFF is saved directly (ImageDescription, DocumentName or XMP), or through an embedded ICC profile, which survives `copy()` in `im.info`. The bytes libtiff skips for alignment are never initialised, so any compressed TIFF over 64 KiB written this way also leaks one stale heap byte per padding hole. That leak needs no crafted tag.

The attached reproducer builds a 131 KB PackBits TIFF and runs `Image.open(...).save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")`. Saving the same image to a file path succeeds, but the `BytesIO` save aborts with glibc's `malloc(): corrupted top size`. A second part of the script shows uninitialised heap bytes at the padding offsets of a `BytesIO` save that are zero in the file save. Saves to real files are unaffected. The defect dates to e782fe721e01 (2013) and has been present since Pillow 2.0.0.

## Details

When `im.save()` writes a TIFF through libtiff to a target that has no usable `fileno()` (`io.BytesIO`, an HTTP response object, a storage backend stream), libtiff is opened with `TIFFClientOpen()` on Pillow's own in-memory sink, `_tiffWriteProc` / `_tiffSeekProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. libtiff treats that sink like a file: when it writes the directory it seeks *beyond* the current end of data (to `eof + IFD size`, where the out-of-line tag values go, and one byte further after every odd-length tag value to keep offsets even) and writes there. On a real file the kernel grows the file and zero-fills the gap. The memory sink does neither correctly:

1. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of `state->loc + size`, so the first write after such a seek can land past the end of the new allocation — a heap buffer overflow whose content is tag data taken from the image being saved.
2. The bytes that libtiff skips are never written, and the grown region is a bare `realloc()`, so they reach the output TIFF with whatever the heap held before.

Both are reachable with default settings by the ordinary "re-encode the upload" sequence `Image.open(upload); im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")` with no save options: `compression` defaults to the source file's (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1734`), any compression other than raw selects the libtiff writer (`:1746`), the source's `tag_v2` entries are passed through to libtiff (`:1959`), and a target without `fileno()` leaves `_fp = 0` (`:1928-1935`), i.e. the memory sink. The overflow half additionally needs an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value of the right length to reach libtiff. With the opened `TiffImageFile` saved directly (`tag_v2` passthrough) that can be a ~64 KiB ASCII tag (269/270/271/272) or the XMP packet (tag 700, type BYTE — arbitrary bytes), and the number of tags the upload carries sets the IFD size, i.e. the overrun length (12 bytes per entry; 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD observed). After `convert()`/`resize()`/`thumbnail()`/`copy()` the `tag_v2` entries are gone, but `im.info["compression"]` (still selecting libtiff) and `im.info["icc_profile"]` survive and the ICC profile is written as tag 34675 (`:1822-1824`), an equally attacker-controlled out-of-line value: `Image.open(x).copy().save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` with the payload in the ICC profile produces the identical ASan report. The stale-byte half needs no attacker tag at all.

**Proof (overflow).** A 131 198-byte hand-built TIFF — mode L, 7×8191, `Compression=32773` (PackBits), an `ImageDescription` of 65 535 characters — opened with `Image.open()` and saved with `im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")` aborts a stock build with glibc's `malloc(): corrupted top size`. The same call against an AddressSanitizer build of the C extensions reports

```
AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ... WRITE of size 65536
 #1 _tiffWriteProc src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:115
 #4 TIFFFlush
 #5 ImagingLibTiffEncode src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056
0 bytes to the right of 131072-byte region, allocated by realloc in _tiffWriteProc src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:103
```

**Proof (uninitialised bytes).** Saving one 300×300 RGB image as `compression="tiff_lzw"` with four odd-length ASCII tags to a `BytesIO`, once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=1` (glibc fills fresh allocations with 0xfe) and once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` (0x55), gives two 369 463-byte TIFFs that differ in exactly 4 bytes, 0xfe vs 0x55, at offsets 369177, 369417, 369423, 369451 — the pad byte between the odd-length last strip and the IFD, and the pad byte after each odd-length tag value except the last. The same save to a filename gives byte-identical files with 0x00 there. Without any allocator tweaks, after a few 64 KB–400 KB Python `bytes` objects filled with 0xa7 are created and freed, re-saving an uploaded LZW TIFF carrying ten odd-length ASCII tags yields 0xa7 at all nine pad offsets.

### Code walk-through

The sink's state is `{data, size (allocated), loc (position), eof (high-water mark)}`; the encoder path starts it as a zeroed 64 KiB block (`TiffDecode.c:863`, `calloc(bufsize, 1)` with `bufsize = 64*1024`, `flrealloc = 1`). Seeking is unconstrained:

```c
/* src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:124-141  _tiffSeekProc */
    case 0: state->loc = off;            break;   /* may exceed eof and size */
    case 1: state->loc += off;           break;
    case 2: state->loc = state->eof + off; break;
```

and writing assumes `loc <= size`:

```c
/* src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:90-117  _tiffWriteProc */
    to_write = MIN(size, state->size - (tsize_t)state->loc);   /* negative if loc > size */
    if (state->flrealloc && size > to_write) {
        tsize_t newsize = state->size;
        while (newsize < (size + state->size)) {               /* capacity target ignores loc */
            …
            newsize += 64 * 1024;
        }
        new_data = realloc(state->data, newsize);              /* tail left uninitialised */
        …
        state->size = newsize;
        to_write = size;
    }
    _TIFFmemcpy((UINT8 *)state->data + state->loc, buf, to_write);   /* :115 */
    state->loc += (toff_t)to_write;
    state->eof = MAX(state->loc, state->eof);
```

A gdb trace of the sink calls during the overflowing save (stock build, breakpoints on the two procs) shows how libtiff drives it:

```
write size=63064 at loc=8      (eof=8     size=65536)     strip data (PackBits re-encode:
write size=2464  at loc=63072  (eof=63072 size=65536)      8 bytes/row × 8191 rows)
seek  off=0     whence=2       -> loc=65536 = eof = size   TIFFWriteDirectory: end of data, already even
seek  off=4;  write size=4 at loc=4                        link IFD offset into header
seek  off=65662 whence=0       (eof=65536 size=65536)      65536 + 126-byte IFD (10 entries) = tag data area
write size=65536 at loc=65662  (eof=65536 size=65536)      ImageDescription, first out-of-line value
```

For that last call `to_write = 65536 − 65662 = −126`, the loop grows `newsize` until it is ≥ `65536 + 65536`, i.e. to 131072, and the `memcpy` writes `[65662, 131198)` into a 131072-byte block: 126 bytes past the end, containing the last 126 bytes of the description string. `loc`/`eof` become 131198 > `size`; `ImagingLibTiffEncode` later sets `size = eof` (`:1067`) and copies `[0, eof)` out of the same block (`:1073`), reading past it as well.

The general condition is: at directory-write time the strip data ends within *IFD-size* bytes of the current allocation boundary, and the first out-of-line tag value has a length just below a multiple of 64 KiB. The overrun length is `IFD size + pad − slack`, so it grows by 12 bytes per additional tag. For single-band images (L, P, 1, I;16, F…) `BitsPerSample` is stored inline and the first out-of-line value in tag order is `DocumentName` (269) or `ImageDescription` (270) — both free-length ASCII strings taken from the source file. Pillow re-encodes the pixels itself, but with PackBits the compressed size is a deterministic function of attacker-chosen pixel rows (the reproducer uses rows of 7 distinct bytes → 8 bytes per row → exactly 65536 bytes including the 8-byte header), so the attacker controls both quantities. For multi-band images the 6-byte `BitsPerSample` array is written first and absorbs the growth, which is why RGB sources do not hit the overflow.

The disclosure half is the benign version of the same sequence. In the LZW/RGB trace the strip data ends at the odd offset 369177; libtiff places the IFD at 369178 and the tag values from 369364 on, and after each odd-length value seeks one byte forward before the next write (`seek off=369418 (loc=369417)`, `write size=5 at loc=369418`, …). Offsets 369177, 369417, 369423 and 369451 are therefore never written. They lie in the part of the buffer obtained by the `realloc()` calls at `:103` (the block grew 65536 → 196608 → 327680 → 458752 during the strip writes), which is not cleared, so the emitted file carries the previous heap contents at those positions. Holes that fall inside the initial 64 KiB are zero only because that block is `calloc`'d.

The defect was introduced in e782fe721e01 ("initial merge of wiredfool/Python-Imaging-Library-G4-Tiff-Support", 2013-03-08), first released in Pillow 2.0.0.

## Impact

Any service that accepts an image and produces a TIFF rendition into a non-file object — the usual pattern for returning or uploading the result without touching disk — is exposed to whoever supplies the image, with no non-default Pillow setting involved. The overflow additionally requires that an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value reaches libtiff: the uploaded ImageDescription/DocumentName/XMP when the application saves the opened TIFF itself (or copies its tags into the save), or the embedded ICC profile, which survives `convert()`/`resize()`/`thumbnail()`/`copy()` in `im.info` together with the compression. Under those conditions, with a crafted single-band TIFF the uploader gets a heap out-of-bounds write in the worker process of IFD-size bytes (12 bytes per directory entry the upload carries — 126 bytes with the minimal reproducer, 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD) immediately past a 128 KiB-class `realloc` block, with the overwritten bytes being the tail of a tag value they chose; on the stock build the minimal reproducer is detected by glibc and kills the process (`SIGABRT`).

Given two addresses leaked by a separate bug, this write has been turned into code execution against a stock build of this commit with ASLR/PIE/NX enabled and default settings (that proof-of-concept is not included with this report): a single-process stdlib `http.server` worker doing nothing but `Image.open(BytesIO(body)).save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` per upload executed an attacker-chosen shell command (`id>/tmp/r.XXXXXX`), answered `200` and kept serving (12/12 against a freshly started worker, 2/6 after twenty unrelated uploads; a miss normally leaves the worker running and is retryable). The two addresses (`&system`, `&PyBytes_Type`) were taken from an unrelated information disclosure in the same process; everything else is this bug plus properties of Pillow's TIFF reader used as a heap-shaping script. The 4.7 MB attack TIFF is a 397×165 8-bit PackBits image whose rows re-encode to exactly 65 528 bytes (strip ends at sink offset 65 536), a 63 942-byte XMP packet (tag 700) as the first out-of-line value, and ~500 private IFD entries. Because `TiffImagePlugin` turns every IFD entry into one `bytes` object in IFD order, frees an earlier entry when a later one repeats its tag number, and parses the IFD three times per request (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1258`, `:1271`, and `getexif()` from `load_end()` at `:1331`), those entries drain glibc's free lists, punch exact-size holes for every large allocation the save makes, and arrange that the 128 KiB `realloc` of the sink lands directly below a live 0x540 chunk followed by libtiff's own `TIFF` handle (`malloc(1313)` from `TIFFClientOpen`). The 2384 overflowing bytes rewrite the start of the `TIFF` struct with the command string, a zeroed `tif_dir`, `tif_diroff = 65536`, and `tif_cleanup = system` at +0x3f8; libtiff resumes `TIFFWriteDirectorySec` on the modified handle and calls `(*tif->tif_cleanup)(tif)`. With gdb on `__libc_system` the call arrives as `__libc_system("id>/tmp/r.…") ← libtiff.so.6 ← TIFFFlush ← ImagingLibTiffEncode (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056) ← _encode (src/encode.c:139)`. Offsets are per-binary constants (glibc 2.36, CPython 3.12.14, libtiff 4.5.0, this `_imaging.so`), all obtainable from public distribution files.

Independently, every compressed TIFF written to such a target that exceeds 64 KiB discloses one byte of stale heap per alignment hole (one per odd-length tag value plus possibly one before the IFD; the count is set by the tags in the uploaded file) at predictable offsets in the returned file — low bandwidth, but it is other requests' freed data. File-path and real-fd targets (`TIFFFdOpen`) are unaffected by either issue. The primitive is the same class and attacker position as the `TiffDecode.c` decode-side heap overflows CVE-2020-35654, CVE-2021-25289 and CVE-2020-10379, but on the encode path and behind the output-to-a-non-file and tag-passthrough preconditions above, with code execution additionally depending on an address leak from another bug.

## Reproducing

`repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow, writes its inputs into a temporary directory. It has two parts. Each part compares saving to a file path, which goes through `TIFFFdOpen` and is correct, with the same save into an `io.BytesIO`, which goes through the `_tiffWriteProc` memory sink.

**Part 1: heap overflow.** `setup_env()` builds `upload.tif` (131 198 bytes) byte by byte: a mode L, 7×8191 image with `Compression=32773` (PackBits) and a 65 535-character `ImageDescription`. The sizes are picked so that when Pillow re-encodes the pixels, the strip comes to 8 + 8191 × 8 = 65 536 bytes and ends exactly at the sink's initial 64 KiB buffer. libtiff then seeks past the 126-byte IFD and writes the 65 536-byte description at offset 65 662. The sink grows only to 131 072 bytes, so the last 126 bytes of the description are written past the end of the heap block. In a fresh child process, the script runs `Image.open("upload.tif").save(<target>, "TIFF")` with no options, once with `"out.tif"` as the target and once with `io.BytesIO()`. The file save exits with 0. The BytesIO save is killed by SIGABRT, with glibc reporting `malloc(): corrupted top size`.

**Part 2: stale heap bytes in the output.** A child started with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` (glibc fills fresh allocations with 0x55) saves a seeded-noise 300×300 RGB image with `compression="tiff_lzw"` and four odd-length ASCII tags. It saves once to a file and once to a BytesIO, then prints every offset where the two outputs differ. libtiff skips one pad byte before the IFD and one after each odd-length tag value. The file has 0x00 at those offsets, but the BytesIO output still holds the 0x55 that was in uninitialised `realloc()` memory.

Expected output on this tree:

```
upload.tif: 131198 bytes
save to file path : exit code 0, out.tif = 131210 bytes
save to BytesIO   : exit code -6, stderr: 'malloc(): corrupted top size'
-> heap overflow crashed the process: True

same image, same options, saved to a file path vs. to a BytesIO:
  offset 369177: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55
  offset 369417: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55
  offset 369423: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55
  offset 369451: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55

-> BytesIO output contains never-written heap bytes: True

BUG
```

The last line is `BUG` if either part shows its defect, and `OK` otherwise. With the attached patch applied and rebuilt, the BytesIO save exits with 0, the two outputs are identical, and the script prints `OK`.

## Suggested fix

The attached patch makes `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` honour sparse-file semantics: it sizes the buffer from the write position, and zeroes what `realloc()` adds (the initial block is already `calloc`'d, so every byte libtiff skips then reads as 0, exactly as through `TIFFFdOpen`). For the non-reallocating case (`flrealloc == 0`), where `loc > size` would also make `to_write` negative, it rejects the write with a `TIFFError`, the same idiom `_tiffReadProc` uses:

```diff
-        while (newsize < (size + state->size)) {
+        while (newsize < (size + (tsize_t)state->loc)) {
 …
+        memset((UINT8 *)new_data + state->size, 0, newsize - state->size);
         state->data = new_data;
         state->size = newsize;
         to_write = size;
+    } else if (to_write < 0) {
+        TIFFError("_tiffWriteProc", "Invalid Write at loc %" PRIu64 ", size: %" PRIu64, …);
+        return 0;
     }
```

`_tiffSeekProc` is left unconstrained, since libtiff legitimately seeks past the end of data; with the write proc fixed, `eof` can no longer exceed `size`, so the read-out in `ImagingLibTiffEncode` (`:1067`, `:1073`) stays within the block. The patch also adds `test_save_bytesio_seek_past_end` to `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py`, which saves the PackBits 64 KiB-boundary case and an LZW case with odd-length tags to both a file and a `BytesIO` and asserts the outputs are identical. With the patch applied and rebuilt, the BytesIO output is byte-identical to the file output, no AddressSanitizer report is produced for tag lengths 65410/65535/131071/196607, the code-execution chain described under Impact no longer runs its command, and the existing TIFF tests pass.

units.body:
urllib3's Proxy-Authorization request header isn't stripped during cross-origin redirects
When using urllib3's proxy support with `ProxyManager`, the `Proxy-Authorization` header is only sent to the configured proxy, as expected.

However, when sending HTTP requests *without* using urllib3's proxy support, it's possible to accidentally configure the `Proxy-Authorization` header even though it won't have any effect as the request is not using a forwarding proxy or a tunneling proxy. In those cases, urllib3 doesn't treat the `Proxy-Authorization` HTTP header as one carrying authentication material and thus doesn't strip the header on cross-origin redirects.

Because this is a highly unlikely scenario, we believe the severity of this vulnerability is low for almost all users. Out of an abundance of caution urllib3 will automatically strip the `Proxy-Authorization` header during cross-origin redirects to avoid the small chance that users are doing this on accident.

Users should use urllib3's proxy support or disable automatic redirects to achieve safe processing of the `Proxy-Authorization` header, but we still decided to strip the header by default in order to further protect users who aren't using the correct approach.

## Affected usages

We believe the number of usages affected by this advisory is low. It requires all of the following to be true to be exploited:

* Setting the `Proxy-Authorization` header without using urllib3's built-in proxy support.
* Not disabling HTTP redirects.
* Either not using an HTTPS origin server or for the proxy or target origin to redirect to a malicious origin.

## Remediation

* Using the `Proxy-Authorization` header with urllib3's `ProxyManager`.
* Disabling HTTP redirects using `redirects=False` when sending requests.
* Not using the `Proxy-Authorization` header.

units.body:
Remote Code Execution in Spring Framework
Spring Framework prior to versions 5.2.20 and 5.3.18 contains a remote code execution vulnerability known as `Spring4Shell`. 

## Impact

A Spring MVC or Spring WebFlux application running on JDK 9+ may be vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE) via data binding. The specific exploit requires the application to run on Tomcat as a WAR deployment. If the application is deployed as a Spring Boot executable jar, i.e. the default, it is not vulnerable to the exploit. However, the nature of the vulnerability is more general, and there may be other ways to exploit it.

These are the prerequisites for the exploit:
- JDK 9 or higher
- Apache Tomcat as the Servlet container
- Packaged as WAR
- `spring-webmvc` or `spring-webflux` dependency

## Patches

- Spring Framework [5.3.18](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-framework/releases/tag/v5.3.18) and [5.2.20](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-framework/releases/tag/v5.2.20.RELEASE)
- Spring Boot [2.6.6](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/releases/tag/v2.6.6) and [2.5.12](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/releases/tag/v2.5.12)

## Workarounds

For those who are unable to upgrade, leaked reports recommend setting `disallowedFields` on `WebDataBinder` through an `@ControllerAdvice`. This works generally, but as a centrally applied workaround fix, may leave some loopholes, in particular if a controller sets `disallowedFields` locally through its own `@InitBinder` method, which overrides the global setting.

To apply the workaround in a more fail-safe way, applications could extend `RequestMappingHandlerAdapter` to update the `WebDataBinder` at the end after all other initialization. In order to do that, a Spring Boot application can declare a `WebMvcRegistrations` bean (Spring MVC) or a `WebFluxRegistrations` bean (Spring WebFlux).

units.body:
Decompression-bomb safeguards bypassed when following HTTP redirects (streaming API)
### Impact

urllib3's [streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/2.6.2/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o) is designed for the efficient handling of large HTTP responses by reading the content in chunks, rather than loading the entire response body into memory at once.

urllib3 can perform decoding or decompression based on the HTTP `Content-Encoding` header (e.g., `gzip`, `deflate`, `br`, or `zstd`). When using the streaming API, the library decompresses only the necessary bytes, enabling partial content consumption.

However, for HTTP redirect responses, the library would read the entire response body to drain the connection and decompress the content unnecessarily. This decompression occurred even before any read methods were called, and configured read limits did not restrict the amount of decompressed data. As a result, there was no safeguard against decompression bombs. A malicious server could exploit this to trigger excessive resource consumption on the client (high CPU usage and large memory allocations for decompressed data; CWE-409).

### Affected usages

Applications and libraries using urllib3 version 2.6.2 and earlier to stream content from untrusted sources by setting `preload_content=False` when they do not disable redirects.


### Remediation

Upgrade to at least urllib3 v2.6.3 in which the library does not decode content of redirect responses when `preload_content=False`.

If upgrading is not immediately possible, disable [redirects](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/2.6.2/user-guide.html#retrying-requests) by setting `redirect=False` for requests to untrusted source.

units.body:
Pillow: TarIO negative size field causes infinite CPU-spin loop
### Summary
`TarIO.__init__` does not check that a tar header's size field is positive. A crafted header with a negative size makes it seek backward onto itself. This causes an infinite loop that uses 100% CPU and never returns.

### Details
`TarIO.__init__` reads 512-byte tar headers one at a time, looking for a member with a given name. For each header it reads the size field and skips ahead to the next header:

```python
size = int(s[124:135], 8)
...
self.fh.seek((size + 511) & (~511), io.SEEK_CUR)
```
There is no check that size is zero or more. A tar header can set this field to a negative octal value. For size = -512, the seek offset comes out to exactly -512, which cancels the 512 bytes the loop had just read. The file position goes right back to where this loop step started.

The loop only stops on end of file or when a header name starts with a null byte. Neither happens, since the same header keeps showing up again. The loop never ends on its own.

### Steps to reproduce

This uses Tests/images/hopper.tar, a normal file already in the Pillow test suite. It only changes the size field of the first header.

```python
from PIL import TarIO

with open("Tests/images/hopper.tar", "rb") as f:
    data = bytearray(f.read())

# Set the size field (bytes 124 to 135) to a negative octal value.
# Octal 1000 is 512, so this is size = -512.
data[124:135] = b"  -00001000"

with open("poisoned.tar", "wb") as f:
    f.write(data)

# "does-not-exist" does not match the header name, so TarIO must
# keep scanning. This call never returns.
TarIO.TarIO("poisoned.tar", "does-not-exist")
```

We confirmed this with ps. The process sits at 98 to 100% CPU and never exits on its own. It only stops if killed from outside.

A pytest version of this, using pytest-timeout so the test does not hang forever, is below. On the current code it fails with Failed: Timeout (>3.0s) from pytest-timeout.

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

import pytest

from PIL import TarIO

SOURCE_TAR = "Tests/images/hopper.tar"


@pytest.mark.timeout(3)
def test_negative_size_field_does_not_hang(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    with open(SOURCE_TAR, "rb") as f:
        data = bytearray(f.read())

    data[124:135] = b"  -00001000"  # octal 1000 = decimal 512, negated

    poisoned_tar = tmp_path / "poisoned.tar"
    poisoned_tar.write_bytes(data)

    with pytest.raises((OSError, ValueError)):
        with TarIO.TarIO(str(poisoned_tar), "does-not-exist"):
            pass
```
### Impact

- Availability: an attacker who can get a crafted tar file passed to TarIO.TarIO() can hang the process at full CPU with a file just over 512 bytes.
- Confidentiality: none.
- Integrity: none.
- TarIO is a small helper class. It is not used by Image.open() and is not on the default path most Pillow users hit. An app has to call PIL.TarIO.TarIO(path, member_name) directly for this to matter, which some apps do to read an image out of a tar archive.

Axios: HTTP/2 adapter bypasses configured DNS lookup and proxy controls ## Summary Axios for Node.js does not apply configured DNS lookup or proxy controls when a request uses `httpVersion: 2`. The HTTP/1 adapter path wraps and forwards `config.lookup`, builds normal request options, and applies proxy routing through `setProxy()`. The HTTP/2 path builds a session with `http2.connect()` using only `options.http2Options`, which drops the top-level `lookup`, `agent`, and proxy state. Applications are affected when they allow a user to influence request destinations, enable axios HTTP/2, and rely on axios `lookup` or proxy routing to prevent SSRF or enforce outbound network policy. ## Impact In affected server-side deployments, an attacker can cause axios to connect directly to destinations that the configured resolver or proxy would have rejected. Depending on reachable services, this can expose cloud metadata, internal service responses, or allow state-changing requests to internal systems. This is not an unconditional SSRF in every axios deployment. It requires `httpVersion: 2` and an application-level trust boundary where user-influenced URLs are constrained by `lookup` or proxy policy. ## Affected Functionality Affected: - Node.js HTTP adapter with `httpVersion: 2`. - `config.lookup` supplied as a DNS policy. - Explicit `config.proxy` and environment-derived proxy settings for HTTPS HTTP/2 requests. Not affected: - Browser adapters. - Node HTTP/1 requests, which pass `lookup` to the transport and apply proxy handling. - Applications that validate destination hosts independently before calling axios. ## Technical Details In `lib/adapters/http.js`, the adapter reads `lookup`, wraps it, stores it on the request `options`, and applies `setProxy()` before selecting a transport. For HTTP/2, `http2Transport.request()` builds an authority from `options.protocol`, `options.hostname`, and `options.port`, then calls: ```js const { http2Options, headers } = options; const session = http2Sessions.getSession(authority, http2Options); ``` `lib/helpers/Http2Sessions.js` ultimately calls `http2.connect(authority, options)` with only the `http2Options` object. The configured DNS lookup and the proxy or tunneling agent installed on the top-level request options are not forwarded into that call. Local verification on axios `1.18.1` showed `lookupCalls: 0` while an HTTP/2 request to a local h2 origin succeeded. A second local HTTPS h2 verification with an explicit rejecting HTTP proxy showed the origin received the request and the proxy observed no traffic. ## Proof of Concept of Attack Local constrained demonstration: 1. Start an HTTP/2 server on loopback. 2. Call `axios.get("http://localhost:/internal", { httpVersion: 2, lookup })` where `lookup` throws `EPOLICY`. 3. Observe that the request succeeds and the lookup counter remains `0`. For proxy routing: 1. Start an HTTPS HTTP/2 origin and a local HTTP proxy that rejects every request and CONNECT. 2. Call axios with `httpVersion: 2`, `http2Options: { rejectUnauthorized: false }`, and explicit `proxy`. 3. Observe that the origin receives the request and the proxy receives nothing. Expected safe behavior is that either the lookup policy blocks the request or the proxy observes and rejects the request. ## Workarounds Use the HTTP/1 adapter path for requests that depend on axios `lookup` or proxy controls. Alternatively, enforce destination allow/deny policy before calling axios, outside the adapter transport path.

Original report

 ### Summary I found that Axios does not apply the configured `lookup` function or proxy when a request uses `httpVersion: 2`. The HTTP/1 adapter applies both controls, but the HTTP/2 path connects straight to the URL's hostname using `http2.connect()`. This matters for server applications that accept a user-influenced URL and use a custom DNS lookup or mandatory outbound proxy to prevent SSRF. Switching the Axios instance to HTTP/2 silently removes those controls, allowing the request to reach an address the application intended to block. I reproduced this on the current npm release, Axios 1.18.1. ### Details The HTTP adapter reads and wraps the caller's `lookup` function, builds the normal request options, and calls `setProxy()`: - `lib/adapters/http.js`, around lines 530-578: reads and wraps `lookup` - `lib/adapters/http.js`, around lines 895-954: adds `lookup` to `options` and applies `setProxy()` For HTTP/2, however, the adapter selects `http2Transport`. That transport creates an authority from the destination and only passes `options.http2Options` to the session pool: ```js const { http2Options, headers } = options; const session = http2Sessions.getSession(authority, http2Options); ``` `lib/helpers/Http2Sessions.js` then calls: ```js const session = http2.connect(authority, options); ``` At this point `options` is only the `http2Options` object. The top-level `lookup`, the proxy tunnelling agent created by `setProxy()`, and the selected `httpAgent`/`httpsAgent` are not forwarded. The request therefore uses the system resolver and opens a direct connection to the origin. The same root cause affects both explicit proxy configuration and environment-derived proxy configuration. I kept the PoC local and used an explicit proxy so the result does not depend on shell environment variables. ### PoC I attached [axios_http2_transport_controls_poc.mjs](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lKXBOLDoysOFRmaRyV1tMVLx3P0Ah4gV/view?usp=sharing). The PoC is entirely local and sets up three pieces: 1. An HTTPS origin with HTTP/2 enabled. If reached, it records the request and returns `REACHED_BLOCKED_ORIGIN`. 2. An HTTP proxy that records traffic but rejects every normal request and every CONNECT request with `502 Bad Gateway`. 3. A custom Axios `lookup` callback that rejects every DNS lookup with an `EPOLICY` error. The first request is an HTTP/1 control request. It uses the blocking `lookup` callback and has proxying disabled. Axios calls the callback, receives `EPOLICY`, and does not reach the origin. This confirms that the callback works and that the hostname is blocked through the normal adapter path. The second request targets the same URL with `httpVersion: 2`. It is given both security controls: the same blocking `lookup` callback and the rejecting proxy. If Axios honors either one, this request cannot reach the origin. It should fail with `EPOLICY`, or it should reach the proxy and receive its `502` response. Instead, the request returns HTTP 200 with `REACHED_BLOCKED_ORIGIN`. The lookup counter does not increase, and the proxy records no request or CONNECT attempt. The origin is the only server that records traffic. This shows that the HTTP/2 path skipped both controls and connected directly using the system resolver. To reproduce, run the attachment from the root of an Axios checkout: Run it from the root of an Axios checkout: ```bash git checkout v1.18.1 npm install --ignore-scripts node /path/to/axios_http2_transport_controls_poc.mjs ``` Relevant output from my run: ```json { "axiosVersion": "1.18.1", "configuredControls": { "lookup": "reject every DNS lookup with EPOLICY", "proxy": "http://127.0.0.1: (reject every request)" }, "http1Control": "EPOLICY: blocked by application DNS policy", "http2Result": { "status": 200, "data": "REACHED_BLOCKED_ORIGIN" }, "lookupCalls": 1, "proxyObservedTraffic": false, "events": [ { "server": "origin", "protocol": "h2", "path": "/internal" } ] } ``` The important parts of the output are: - `http1Control` contains `EPOLICY`, proving the DNS policy blocks the destination under HTTP/1. - `lookupCalls` is still `1` after both requests, proving HTTP/2 never called the configured resolver. - `proxyObservedTraffic` is `false`, proving HTTP/2 did not use the configured proxy. - `http2Result.status` is `200`, and the sole event belongs to the origin, proving Axios connected directly to the blocked destination. ### Impact The vulnerable configuration is a Node.js application that: - enables Axios HTTP/2 using `httpVersion: 2`; - lets an application user influence the request destination; and - relies on Axios's `lookup` option or proxy routing to enforce a destination or egress policy. In that setup, an unauthenticated application user may be able to make the server connect directly to loopback, private-network, or link-local services that the lookup policy or proxy would have rejected. Depending on the reachable service, this can expose cloud credentials or internal data, modify internal services, or affect availability. HTTP/2 support is marked experimental, but neither the HTTP/2 documentation nor the proxy documentation says that `lookup` and proxy controls are ignored. The proxy documentation states that HTTPS requests are sent through a CONNECT tunnel. More importantly, Axios's threat model tells callers that destination validation is their responsibility; this behavior silently bypasses such caller-supplied validation. I did not test against any third-party or production service. The PoC only uses listeners on my own machine.
---

Apache Log4j Core: Silent log event loss in XmlLayout due to unescaped XML 1.0 forbidden characters
Apache Log4j Core's [`XmlLayout`](https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/manual/layouts.html#XmlLayout), in versions up to and including 2.25.3, fails to sanitize characters forbidden by the [XML 1.0 specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/#charsets), producing invalid XML output whenever a log message or MDC value contains such characters.

The impact depends on the StAX implementation in use:

Users are advised to upgrade to Apache Log4j Core 2.25.4, which corrects this issue by sanitizing forbidden characters before XML output.

units.body:
Axios: Excessive recursion in formDataToJSON can cause denial of service
## Summary
Axios versions `0.28.0` and later contain uncontrolled recursion in `formDataToJSON`, the helper behind the public `axios.formToJSON()` / named `formToJSON` API and the default request transform used when FormData is sent with an `application/json` content type.

Applications are affected when they pass attacker-controlled `FormData` field names into this functionality. A field name with thousands of nested bracket segments can exhaust the JavaScript call stack and throw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, causing request failure and, in applications that do not handle the exception or rejected promise, possible process termination.

## Impact
The impact is denial of service against applications that process untrusted `FormData` field names through axios' FormData-to-JSON conversion.

The vulnerable path is not reached by merely installing axios, by normal multipart `FormData` pass-through, or by ordinary axios requests that do not request JSON serialisation of `FormData`. In the default axios request, the error is produced before network I/O and returned as a rejected Promise. Direct use of `formToJSON()` throws synchronously.

Server-side applications are the primary risk when remote users can submit arbitrary form field names, and the application converts those fields with `formToJSON()` or sends them through axios as JSON.

## Affected Functionality
Affected APIs and paths:
- `axios.formToJSON(formData)`
- `import { formToJSON } from "axios"`
- `lib/helpers/formDataToJSON.js`
- axios default `transformRequest` when `data` is `FormData` and `Content-Type` contains `application/json`

Unaffected or lower-risk paths:
- Normal multipart `FormData` requests without `JSON Content-Type`
- `toFormData()` object-to-FormData serialisation, which already has a `maxDepth` guard
- Axios versions before 0.28.0, where this helper and public API were not present

## Technical Details
`lib/helpers/formDataToJSON.js` parses a form field name into path segments with `parsePropPath()`. For a key such as `a[x][x][x]`, each bracketed segment becomes another path element.

`formDataToJSON()` then calls the nested `buildPath(path, value, target, index)` function. `buildPath()` recursively calls itself once for each path segment and does not enforce a maximum depth:

`const result = buildPath(path, value, target[name], index);`

A key containing thousands of bracket segments, therefore, creates thousands of recursive calls. At sufficient depth, V8 throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`.

Axios already applies a depth guard to the inverse serializer in `lib/helpers/toFormData.js`, where `maxDepth` defaults to 100 and exceeding it throws `AxiosError` with code `ERR_FORM_DATA_DEPTH_EXCEEDED`. `formDataToJSON()` does not currently have equivalent protection.

## Proof of Concept of Attack
```js
import { formToJSON } from "axios";

const fd = new FormData();
fd.append("a" + "[x]".repeat(15000), "value");

try {
  formToJSON(fd);
  console.log("not vulnerable");
} catch (err) {
  console.log(`${err.constructor.name}: ${err.message}`);
}
```

Expected vulnerable result:

RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded

The axios request transform path can also be reached before network I/O:

```js
import axios from "axios";

const fd = new FormData();
fd.append("a" + "[x]".repeat(15000), "value");

await axios
  .post("http://127.0.0.1:1/", fd, {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }
  })
  .catch((err) => console.log(`${err.constructor.name}: ${err.message}`));
```

Expected vulnerable result:

RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded

## Workarounds
Applications can avoid the vulnerable path by not converting attacker-controlled `FormData` to JSON with axios.

If conversion is required before a fixed axios release is available, validate `FormData` field names before calling `formToJSON()` or before sending `FormData` with `Content-Type: application/json`. Reject keys whose parsed nesting depth exceeds the application's expected schema.

For axios requests carrying untrusted `FormData`, avoid setting `Content-Type: application/json`; leaving the data as multipart FormData bypasses `formDataToJSON()`.

Catching the resulting error can prevent process termination, but it does not remove the uncontrolled-recursion behaviour and should not be treated as the primary mitigation.
